weeks.title: What is AI Automation?
weeks.context:
AI automation is the practice of combining AI models (language models, vision models, classification models) with workflow orchestration to replace or augment repetitive, judgment-heavy tasks that previously required a human. It is not RPA (Robotic Process Automation), clicking through UIs with a script, though it can include that. It is not just calling an API and displaying the result. AI automation is building systems that can perceive input, reason about it, act on it, and handle the variation that human workers handle.

The economic model is simple: if a task costs $X per hour and takes Y hours per week, and an AI automation can do it for $0.01 per run in 30 seconds, the business case is obvious. Your job as an AI automation builder is to identify those tasks, build the automations reliably, and deliver them to clients or employers as working systems.

This week you map the landscape: what can AI automation do today (document extraction, classification, drafting, research, data transformation), what it cannot do reliably yet (tasks requiring physical world interaction, novel judgment in high-stakes domains), and what the full toolchain looks like from trigger to output.

items.title: Git, version control from day 1
items.body:
## The one picture that prevents 90% of Git confusion

Git keeps your work in three places, and almost every beginner mistake comes from not knowing which one you are touching:

- **Working directory** is the files on your computer right now, exactly as you are editing them.
- **Staging area** is a holding tray for the precise changes you want in your next snapshot.
- **History** is the permanent timeline of snapshots you have already saved.

A **commit** moves changes from the staging area into history. A **push** copies that history up to GitHub so it lives somewhere other than your laptop. Every command below is just moving your work between these places. Hold this picture in your head and the commands stop feeling random.

## What Git is and why every team uses it

Git is the version-control tool behind essentially every codebase past day one. It snapshots your project after each meaningful change so you can see exactly what changed, undo a mistake without losing everything else, and work alongside other people without overwriting each other. You will use it every single day on this track, and the handful of commands below cover about 95% of daily work.

## Install Git and tell it who you are

```bash
# macOS:   brew install git
# Windows: winget install Git.Git   (or download from git-scm.com)
# Linux:   sudo apt install git

git --version
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
```

`git --version` prints something like `git version 2.43.0`. If you instead see `command not found`, Git is not installed yet. Install it, then reopen your terminal so the new program is found.

The two `config` lines touch no project at all. They write your identity into a settings file in your home folder so every future commit is stamped with who made it. Skip them and your very first commit dies with `Author identity unknown`.

## The five commands you will actually use

```bash
git init               # turn the current folder into a Git repo
git status             # what has changed since the last commit?
git add file.py        # move one change into the staging area
git commit -m "msg"    # save everything staged as one snapshot
git log --oneline      # the list of snapshots, newest first
```

Walk them in the order you would really use them:

- `git init` creates a hidden `.git` folder, and that folder *is* the repo. You run it once per project. It prints `Initialized empty Git repository`.
- `git status` is the command you will run most. It shows which files changed and whether they are staged yet. Run it whenever you are unsure what state you are in, because it never changes anything itself.
- `git add file.py` moves that file's changes into staging. Nothing is saved yet, you are only choosing what goes into the next snapshot. Use `git add .` to stage everything at once.
- `git commit -m "msg"` writes everything staged into history as one snapshot. The `-m` flag is your one-line note to your future self about what changed. It prints something like `1 file changed, 3 insertions(+)`.
- `git log --oneline` prints one short line per commit so you can read the trail of your work. Press `q` to leave the log view.

## Push it to GitHub so it survives your laptop

```bash
# after creating an empty repo on github.com:
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOU/your-repo.git
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main
```

- `git remote add origin ...` saves GitHub's URL under the nickname `origin`. From here on, `origin` simply means "the GitHub copy."
- `git branch -M main` renames your current branch to `main` so it matches what GitHub expects.
- `git push -u origin main` uploads your commits to GitHub. The `-u` flag links your local `main` to GitHub's copy so that next time you can just type `git push`. Refresh the GitHub page and your files are there.

## When it breaks, and it will

- `Author identity unknown` means you skipped the two `git config` lines above. Run them, then commit again.
- `fatal: not a git repository` means you are not inside a repo folder. `cd` into the project, or run `git init` first.
- `failed to push some refs` means GitHub has a commit your laptop does not. Run `git pull` to merge it down, then push again.
- `nothing to commit, working tree clean` is not an error. Git is telling you there are no staged changes to save right now.

## Where Git shows up next

Every project on this track ships to GitHub, and every check-in you submit is backed by a commit. This is a prerequisite for everything that follows. Read it once now, and come back to it any time you are unsure which of the three places your work is currently sitting in.

items.title: Docker, containers in 10 minutes
items.body:
## What Docker is
Docker packages your application + its OS dependencies into a single immutable image that runs the same on your laptop, on CI, and in production. "Works on my machine" stops happening.

## The three nouns
- **Image**, a blueprint. Built from a Dockerfile. Stored in a registry (Docker Hub, GHCR).
- **Container**, a running instance of an image. Multiple containers can run from the same image.
- **Dockerfile**, the text recipe describing how to build the image.

## Smallest possible Dockerfile
```dockerfile
FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
CMD ["python", "main.py"]
```

## The five commands you actually use
```bash
docker build -t myapp . # build the image from ./Dockerfile
docker run -p 8000:8000 myapp # run it; map container port 8000 to host
docker ps # what's running?
docker logs <container_id> # what is it saying?
docker stop <container_id> # graceful stop
```

## When you'll see Docker next
This track containerises one or more services later in the roadmap. The five commands above are all you need to read the rest.

items.title: NumPy, the array library underneath every Python data tool
items.body:
## What NumPy is
NumPy is the Python library for fast typed arrays. It is the bedrock under pandas, scikit-learn, PyTorch, TensorFlow. If you do data work in Python, you use NumPy, often through other libraries that wrap it.

## Install + import
```bash
pip install numpy
```
```python
import numpy as np # the universal alias
```

## NumPy array vs Python list
A list holds anything. An array holds ONE type only and lives in contiguous memory, that's why NumPy is 10-100× faster than equivalent list code.

```python
py = [1, 2, 3] ; np_arr = np.array([1, 2, 3])
py * 2 # [1,2,3,1,2,3] np_arr * 2 # array([2, 4, 6]) <- ELEMENT-WISE
```

That element-wise behaviour is the whole game, arithmetic on arrays vectorises with no `for` loop.

## The dot product (a.k.a. `@`), the operation half this track uses
```python
a = np.array([2.3, 17.0, 4.0])
b = np.array([3.0, 0.1, -0.2])
a @ b # 7.8
np.dot(a, b) # 7.8 -- same thing; `@` is the modern syntax
```

## The surface this track actually needs from you
- `np.array([...])`, create.
- `a @ b` or `np.dot(a, b)`, dot product.
- `np.linalg.norm(v)`, vector length.
- Element-wise arithmetic, no loops needed.

That is the whole prerequisite. The rest you learn as you meet it.

items.title: Which AI provider should you use?
items.body:
## Which AI provider should you use?

Many automations in this course call an AI model for the "thinking" step (extracting, classifying, drafting). You will need a provider. Here is the simple guidance.

**Use OpenAI (`gpt-4o-mini`) as your default.** It has the best support across no-code tools (Zapier, Make, and n8n all ship native OpenAI steps), it is reliable, and it is cheap, cents per run, so a month of building costs a dollar or two. Examples here assume it.

**No credit card? Use a free option:**
- **Ollama** runs an open model (Llama 3) locally: no key, no cost, no internet once downloaded. It is slower, and you call it via its local HTTP endpoint, which n8n and custom code can hit.
- **Google Gemini** has a free tier with a generous request limit, fine for learning.

| | OpenAI gpt-4o-mini | Ollama (local) | Gemini (free tier) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cost | cents per run | free | free (limited) |
| No-code support | best | partial | growing |
| Internet | required | only to download | required |

**Recommendation:** start with OpenAI for the smoothest path and the most working examples; drop to Ollama or Gemini if cost or access is a barrier. The automation skills (wiring steps, handling the output) are identical whichever you pick.

items.title: Zero-cost path (free alternatives)
items.body:
## Zero-cost path (no credit card required)

This week mentions industry-standard tools that can cost money. You can complete every step for free, with no card and no trial that auto-renews:

- **LLM calls**, use **Ollama** (runs Llama 3 / Mistral locally, free, no API key): point the base URL at `http://localhost:11434`. The chat shape is identical; you just swap the endpoint. Hugging Face's free Inference API also needs no credit card.
- **Google Cloud / BigQuery**, use **DuckDB** (local, the same SQL, blazing fast) or local **Postgres**. No GCP account needed.
- **Cloud warehouse**, use **DuckDB** or local **Postgres**: identical SQL, zero cost.

Learn the concept with the free tool; the paid service is only how some teams run it in production. The skills and the code are the same.

items.title: The automation landscape
items.body:
## The automation landscape: what's actually possible today

Before you build anything, you need an honest map of what AI automation can and cannot do, because half of building well is choosing the right problem. Pick a task AI handles reliably and you ship something that runs for months untouched; pick one it handles *almost* reliably and you build a machine that embarrasses you at 2 a.m.

**What AI automation does well today.** The sweet spot is *language-and-judgment work on structured-enough inputs*: extracting fields from invoices, contracts, and resumes; classifying and routing emails or support tickets; drafting replies, summaries, and first-pass reports; researching and enriching data (e.g. "find this company's industry and size"); and transforming messy text into clean, structured records. These share a shape, a human used to read something, make a small judgment, and produce an output. That judgment is exactly what a language model now does cheaply and fast.

**What it does not do reliably yet.** Anything requiring real-world physical action, high-stakes novel judgment (medical, legal, financial decisions with no human review), perfect accuracy with zero tolerance for error, or reasoning over information that simply is not available to the model. The failure mode that bites beginners is the "looks 95% right" task, where the 5% wrong is silent and expensive. Automate those only with a human checkpoint.

**The economics that justify the work.** The pitch is brutally simple: a task that costs a person $30/hour and eats 8 hours a week costs ~$960/month. An automation that does it for cents per run and seconds per item turns that into near-zero. *That gap is your entire business case*, and learning to spot it is the highest-value skill of the week.

Today, orient: write down five repetitive, language-heavy tasks you've seen people do, at a job, in a side hustle, in your own week. Beside each, mark "reliable / risky" using the rules above. Those reliable ones are your future automations.

days.title: No-code vs low-code vs code
days.summary: Understand the three tiers. Know which tool to reach for.

items.title: No-code vs low-code vs code
items.body:
## No-code, low-code, code: pick the right altitude

There are three ways to build an automation, and choosing the wrong one wastes days. They are not ranked by "skill", a senior builder reaches for no-code constantly. They are tools at different altitudes, and the art is matching the tool to the job.

**No-code** (Zapier, Make, n8n's visual editor) means wiring pre-built blocks together in a drag-and-drop canvas: "when a new row appears in this sheet → send it to an AI model → post the result to Slack." You build in minutes, you read the flow at a glance, and a non-programmer can maintain it. The ceiling: when your logic gets genuinely branchy or you need something no block offers, you start fighting the canvas.

**Low-code** (n8n with code nodes, Make with custom functions) is the same visual flow but with small snippets of real code dropped into individual steps. You keep the speed and visibility of no-code but escape its limits exactly where you need to, the pragmatic default for most client work.

**Code** (Python scripts, LangChain, custom services) means writing the whole thing yourself. You get total control, version control, testing, and the ability to build things no platform supports, autonomous agents, complex RAG, custom orchestration. The cost is time, and you own every line forever.

**The decision rule:** start at the *highest* altitude (no-code) and drop down only when the job forces you. A surprising share of paid automations never need to leave Make or n8n. Beginners over-reach for Python out of pride and ship slower; professionals reach for code only when no-code genuinely can't do it.

Today: take the automation idea you sketched yesterday and decide its altitude. Could Make/n8n do it end to end? Where, specifically, might it need a code node? Write the answer, that judgment is what clients pay for.

days.title: How AI fits into automation
days.summary: AI is one step in a pipeline, not the whole pipeline.

items.title: How AI fits into automation
items.body:
## Where AI actually sits in an automation

A common beginner mistake is thinking "AI automation = call ChatGPT." The AI is one component inside a larger pipeline, and understanding the *shape* of that pipeline is what lets you build reliable systems instead of fragile demos.

**The universal pipeline: Trigger → Fetch → AI step → Act.** Every automation, no-code or code, follows this spine. A **trigger** starts it (a new email, a form submission, a schedule, a webhook). A **fetch/prepare** step gathers the input the AI needs (read the email body, pull the attachment, query a record). The **AI step** does the judgment, the language work no rule could do: extract, classify, draft, summarise, decide. Then an **act** step does something with the result (write to a database, send a reply, post to Slack, update a CRM).

**The AI is the brain, not the body.** The model's job is the *one judgment* that used to require a human. Everything around it, the triggering, the data plumbing, the acting, is deterministic glue you control. This split matters because the glue is where reliability lives: validate the AI's output, handle the case where it returns nonsense, retry on a failed API call. A good automation treats the model as a powerful-but-fallible component and wraps it in checks.

**Structured output is the hinge.** The trick that makes AI usable in automation is forcing the model to return *structured* data (JSON with named fields) instead of prose, so the next step can act on it programmatically. "Extract the invoice total" should return `{"total": 1240.50, "currency": "USD"}`, not a friendly paragraph. You'll build this constantly; it's the difference between a chatbot and an automation.

Today: take your automation idea and draw its pipeline, label the trigger, the fetch, the exact AI judgment (in one sentence), and the act. Then write the JSON shape you'd want the AI step to return. You're now thinking like a builder, not a prompter.

items.title: The tools you will learn
items.body:
## The toolchain you'll actually learn

This program builds toward one capability: shipping real AI automations clients pay for. To do that you'll learn a specific, deliberately small toolchain, and knowing the map now stops you from chasing every shiny tool later.

**Orchestration (the canvas).** **n8n** is the spine of the no-code/low-code work, open-source, self-hostable, with both visual blocks and code nodes, so it spans two altitudes in one tool. **Make** (and Zapier) are commercial alternatives you'll meet; the concepts transfer directly. Orchestration tools are where triggers, data flow, and acting live.

**The AI layer (the brain).** You'll call hosted language models through their APIs. **Claude** (Anthropic) and **GPT** (OpenAI) are the two you'll use most; the current top models, Claude Opus 4.8 for the hardest reasoning, Claude Sonnet 4.6 and GPT-class models for the everyday work, and small fast models (Claude Haiku) for cheap high-volume steps, all speak the same basic request/response shape. You'll learn to pick the cheapest model that does the job, because at scale, model choice *is* your margin.

**Code and frameworks.** **Python** is the escape hatch and the language of the back half of the course. **LangChain** and agent frameworks come later for autonomous, multi-step systems. **RAG** (retrieval over your own documents) and **browser/computer automation** round out the advanced toolkit.

**Glue and delivery.** APIs and webhooks connect everything; Git versions your work; and deployment/monitoring tools keep automations running unattended, the part that separates a demo from a product.

The discipline: **learn this stack deeply, ignore the rest.** New automation tools launch weekly; the concepts here, trigger, AI judgment, structured output, orchestration, transfer to all of them.

Today: make sure your accounts are live, an n8n instance (cloud or local) and at least one AI provider key, and write a one-line note on which model tier you'd use for a high-volume, low-difficulty step versus a rare, hard one. That cost instinct starts now.

items.title: Your automation idea
items.body:
## Your automation idea: commit to one real build

Everything in the first half of this program threads toward one thing you'll build by Week 10, a real, working automation. Today you choose it. A vague "something with AI" dissolves into nothing; a sharp, specific brief gives every future week a target.

**What makes a good first automation.** It is *real* (solves a task someone actually does repeatedly), *bounded* (one clear trigger, one clear output, not a sprawling platform), and *AI-justified* (the core step genuinely needs language judgment, not just a rule). "Auto-categorise my incoming invoices and log them to a sheet" is a great brief. "Build an AI assistant for my whole business" is not a brief, it's a wish.

**Write the brief, five questions.** (1) **Trigger:** what starts it, a new email, a form, a schedule, a file drop? (2) **Input:** what data does it receive? (3) **AI judgment:** the single sentence describing the human-like decision the model makes, "extract the vendor, amount, and due date", "classify this as urgent or not". (4) **Output/act:** what it produces and where it goes. (5) **Who benefits:** whose time does this save, and roughly how much? That last answer is your future sales pitch.

**Source it from real pain.** The best ideas come from watching someone (or yourself) do something tedious. Freelancers triaging client emails, a small shop copying order details between systems, a recruiter screening resumes, these are everywhere, and they are willing to pay. Pick one where you can actually see the task, so you can build against reality, not imagination.

Today: write your automation brief, the five questions answered concretely, in a file you commit to your repo. Keep it small enough to finish and real enough to matter. You'll return to this brief every week; make it one you'd be proud to demo.

days.title: Day 6 - What is AI Automation?
days.summary: Today you'll spot real automation opportunities, listing the repetitive tasks around you that AI could take over.

items.title: Day 6 - What is AI Automation?
items.body:
## Spotting opportunities: train your automation radar

The single most valuable habit of an AI-automation builder isn't coding, it's *seeing*. Opportunities are everywhere, but only if you've trained yourself to notice the shape of an automatable task. Today you sharpen that radar deliberately.

**The signature of an automatable task.** Look for work that is **repetitive** (done the same way, often), **rule-ish but not pure-rule** (needs a small judgment a plain script can't make), **language- or document-heavy** (reading, writing, extracting, classifying), and **bounded in stakes** (a mistake is recoverable, or a human reviews the output). When all four line up, you're looking at money on the table. Pure-rule tasks ("if amount > 100, flag it") don't need AI; pure-creative or high-stakes-novel tasks aren't ready for it. The gold is in between.

**Where to look.** *Inboxes* (triage, drafting, follow-ups). *Spreadsheets* (data entry, cleaning, enrichment, copying between systems). *Documents* (invoices, contracts, forms, reports, anything someone reads to pull out a few facts). *Repetitive research* ("look up each of these 200 companies"). *Hand-offs between tools* that someone bridges by copy-paste. Each is a pattern you'll meet again and again across clients.

**Quantify, always.** For every opportunity, estimate frequency × time × cost. "This person spends ~6 hours a week, at ~$25/hour, copying order data, that's ~$650/month." The number turns a vague idea into a fundable project and a sales conversation. Builders who can't quantify the saving stay hobbyists; builders who can, close deals.

Today: do a structured opportunity hunt. List **ten** repetitive tasks you can observe around you, your work, your family's small business, online communities complaining about busywork. Score each against the four-signal test and slap a rough monthly-cost estimate on the top three. This list is a pipeline of future paid work, keep adding to it for the rest of the program.

items.title: Day 7 - What is AI Automation?
items.body:
## Ship it: your Week 1 artefact

Wrap the week with a real, committed artefact, not notes in your head, but a written plan in your repo that you could hand to a client or an employer. Shipping something small every week is the habit that turns a 20-week course into a portfolio.

**What to produce this week.** A single, well-structured document, `automation-plan.md`, in your course repo, containing:
- **The chosen automation brief**: trigger, input, the one-sentence AI judgment, output/act, and who benefits (with a rough monthly-cost saving).
- **The pipeline sketch**: Trigger → Fetch → AI step → Act, with the JSON shape you want the AI step to return.
- **The altitude decision**: no-code, low-code, or code, and *why*, including where it might need a code node.
- **Your opportunity list**: the ten tasks from Day 6 with the top three quantified. This is your future pipeline.

**Commit it like a professional.** Clean message, real repo:

```bash
git add automation-plan.md opportunity-list.md
git commit -m "Week 1: AI automation plan + opportunity pipeline"
git push
```

**Why this matters.** You haven't built the automation yet, and that's correct. This week was about *judgment*, choosing the right task, at the right altitude, with a clear pipeline and a real business case. That judgment is what separates builders who ship reliable, paid automations from people who endlessly tinker with demos. The plan you committed is the foundation everything else is built on.

Next week: you go hands-on, building your first working automation in n8n with no code at all, and seeing the Trigger → AI → Act pipeline run for real.

weeks.title: No-code automation with n8n
weeks.context:
n8n is an open-source workflow automation platform, like Zapier but self-hostable and with a full visual workflow builder. It connects to 400+ services out of the box and lets you write JavaScript in nodes when you need custom logic. For AI automation, n8n is the orchestration layer: it handles the trigger, calls external APIs (including Claude), parses responses, and routes data to the right outputs.

The no-code approach is not a lesser approach, it is faster for many tasks. A workflow that routes incoming Gmail emails based on sentiment, extracts structured data, and adds a row to a Google Sheet should take 20 minutes to build in n8n, not a day in Python. Use the right tool for the complexity of the task.

This week you build 3 complete n8n workflows using Claude: an email classifier that routes support tickets, a document summariser triggered by a webhook, and a daily news digest that pulls from RSS feeds and summarises them.

days.title: Install n8n
days.summary: Get n8n running on your machine.

items.title: Install n8n
items.body:
## Install n8n and meet the canvas

n8n is your orchestration layer for the next stretch, the tool that handles triggers, calls APIs (including Claude), parses responses, and routes data, all in a visual workflow you can read at a glance. Today you get it running and learn to navigate it, because comfort with the canvas is what makes everything after fast.

**Two ways to run it.** *n8n Cloud* is the zero-friction path: sign up, and you're building in minutes, ideal for learning and for client work you don't want to host. *Self-hosted* (via Docker: `docker run -it --rm -p 5678:5678 n8nio/n8n`) is free, private, and the choice when a client's data can't leave their infrastructure. Either way you land on the same editor. Pick cloud now so nothing blocks learning; you'll meet Docker deployment properly in Week 16.

**The mental model: nodes and connections.** A workflow is a graph. Each **node** is one step, a trigger, an action, a transformation, and the **connections** (the lines) carry data from one node to the next. Data flows left to right as a stream of JSON items. Understanding that "everything between nodes is JSON" is the single insight that makes n8n click; every node receives JSON, does something, and passes JSON on.

**Trigger vs action nodes.** Every workflow starts with a **trigger** node (what kicks it off: a schedule, a webhook, a new email) and continues with **action** nodes (do something: call an API, write a row, send a message). You can't have a workflow without a trigger, it's the "when".

**The executions view** is your debugger: it shows each run, which nodes succeeded, and the exact JSON that flowed through each one. You'll live here when something breaks. Learning to read it now saves hours later.

Today: get n8n running, open a blank workflow, add a Manual Trigger and a "Set" node, run it, then open the execution and inspect the JSON that passed between them. You've just seen the data stream that every future automation rides on.

days.title: Your first workflow
days.summary: Trigger → HTTP request → display result.

items.title: Your first workflow
items.body:
## Your first real workflow: Trigger → AI → Act

Today you build the canonical pipeline from Week 1, Trigger → Fetch → AI → Act, for real, in n8n, and watch it run end to end. This is the moment the abstract pipeline becomes a working thing.

**The build.** Start with a **Manual Trigger** (so you can run it on demand while testing). Add a **Set** node to define some input text, pretend it's an incoming support message. Add an **HTTP Request** node (or the dedicated Anthropic node if available) that calls **Claude** with a prompt: "Classify this message as billing, technical, or general, and reply with JSON." Then add a node that uses the result, a **Slack** or **Gmail** node, or just another Set node, to act on the classification.

**Calling the AI: the HTTP Request node.** This node is your universal key to any API. You set the method (POST), the URL (the model's endpoint), the headers (your API key), and the JSON body (the model, the prompt, the parameters). When you learn to call one API this way, you can call *any* of them, this single node is why n8n can do almost anything.

**Wiring the data through with expressions.** n8n's `{{ }}` expressions let one node reference another's output: `{{ $json.message }}` pulls the `message` field from the incoming item. This is how data threads through the workflow, the AI node reads the trigger's text, the act node reads the AI's answer. Expressions are the glue; get comfortable with `$json` referencing the current item.

**Run and inspect.** Execute the workflow and open each node's output. See the message go in, the AI's JSON classification come back, and the act node fire. When it works, you've built a complete AI automation with zero code, exactly the speed advantage no-code gives you.

Today: build this classify-and-act workflow. Send three different test messages through it and confirm each is classified correctly. You now have the core pattern every automation in this course extends.

days.title: Add a transformation step
days.summary: Use the Set node to reshape data.

items.title: Add a transformation step
items.body:
## Transformation: shaping data between steps

Real automations rarely pass data cleanly from one node to the next, the trigger gives you one shape, the AI wants another, the destination wants a third. **Transformation nodes** are where you reshape, filter, and clean the data stream. This is the unglamorous plumbing that makes the difference between a demo and something that survives real inputs.

**The workhorses.** The **Set** node creates or overwrites fields, use it to build exactly the payload the next node needs. The **Edit Fields / Code** node runs small JavaScript when no built-in node fits: `return items.map(i => ({ json: { ...i.json, total: i.json.price * i.json.qty } }))`. The **Filter** node drops items that don't meet a condition (only continue for "urgent" messages). The **IF** / **Switch** nodes branch the flow down different paths based on the data, the AI's classification routes billing emails one way, technical another.

**Items: the unit n8n operates on.** Data flows as an array of **items**, each a JSON object. Many nodes run *once per item* automatically, feed in 50 rows and the AI node fires 50 times, once each. Understanding the item model explains both n8n's power (batch processing for free) and its surprises (why a node ran 50 times and burned 50 API calls). Watch your item counts; they're your cost.

**Parsing AI output.** The model returns text; you often need a field from inside it. If you asked for JSON, a **Code** node with `JSON.parse()` turns the AI's string into structured data your next node can use. This parse step is where "the AI said something" becomes "the workflow can act on it."

Today: extend yesterday's workflow. After the AI classifies the message, add a transformation that parses the JSON, then a **Switch** node that routes "billing" vs "technical" vs "general" to three different end nodes. You've turned a single AI call into a routing engine.

days.title: Add a schedule trigger
days.summary: Make your automation run automatically every hour.

items.title: Add a schedule trigger
items.body:
## Schedule triggers: automations that run without you

So far you've clicked "execute". Real automations run on their own, that's the whole point. The **Schedule Trigger** turns a workflow into something that fires on a clock: every hour, every morning at 8, the first of the month. This is the step that makes an automation an *asset* instead of a tool you operate.

**The Schedule Trigger.** Replace the Manual Trigger with a Schedule Trigger and set an interval (cron syntax for precision: `0 8 * * 1-5` = 8 a.m. on weekdays). When the workflow is **active** (the toggle in the top bar), n8n runs it automatically at each tick, no browser open, no human present. This is the difference between "I run a script" and "a system runs."

**The polling pattern.** A common scheduled design: every N minutes, *check* a source for new items (new rows in a sheet, new files in a folder, new emails), process anything new, and remember what you've already handled so you don't reprocess it. Tracking "what's new" (a timestamp, a status column, a stored ID) is the subtle part, get it wrong and you either miss items or process them twice.

**Schedule vs webhook, two ways to start.** A *schedule* trigger is **pull**: you check on a clock. A *webhook* trigger (tomorrow) is **push**: the source notifies you instantly. Pull is simple and fine when "within an hour" is good enough; push is real-time but needs the source to support it. Choosing between them is a real design decision you'll make on every project.

**Idempotency, the reliability habit.** A scheduled workflow that re-runs should never double-act, sending the same email twice because it ran again before the first finished is a classic, embarrassing bug. Design so that processing the same item twice is safe (check "already done?" before acting).

Today: set yesterday's workflow on a schedule (every 5 minutes while testing), activate it, and watch it fire on its own in the executions view. Then add a guard so the same input isn't processed twice. You've built your first unattended automation.

items.title: Connect to Gmail or Webhook
items.body:
## Connecting to the real world: Gmail and webhooks

An automation is only useful when it's wired to where work actually happens, inboxes, forms, other apps. Today you connect n8n to real services two ways: **Gmail** (a real trigger and a real action) and **webhooks** (the universal connector that lets *anything* start your workflow).

**Gmail (or any 400+ service node).** n8n ships native nodes for hundreds of apps. The **Gmail Trigger** fires when a new email arrives (matching a label or search); the **Gmail** action node sends or replies. Connecting requires **OAuth**, a one-time "allow n8n to access this account" handshake, after which the node just works. Wire a Gmail Trigger → Claude classify → Gmail draft-reply, and you've built the email-triage automation businesses pay for, in minutes.

**Webhooks: the universal front door.** A **Webhook** node gives your workflow a URL. Anything that can make an HTTP request, a website form, another app, a mobile shortcut, a different automation, can hit that URL and instantly trigger your workflow, passing data in the request body. Webhooks are how systems that *don't* have a native n8n node still talk to you. Master webhooks and nothing is truly un-connectable.

**The two halves of integration.** *Receiving* (a trigger node or webhook starts your flow) and *sending* (an action node or HTTP Request reaches out to another system). Every automation is some composition of these. The OAuth-connected nodes handle auth for you; the HTTP Request node + webhook handle everything those nodes don't cover.

**Credentials, handled once and safely.** n8n stores credentials (API keys, OAuth tokens) separately from the workflow, so you connect an account once and reuse it, and you never paste a raw key into a node. This is also why you can share a workflow without leaking secrets.

Today: build a Gmail-triggered workflow that classifies each incoming email with Claude and drafts (not sends, human-in-the-loop) a reply. Send yourself a test email and watch the draft appear. That's a sellable automation, built entirely no-code.

items.title: Day 6 - No-code automation with n8n
items.body:
## Consolidate: make one workflow genuinely robust

You can now build workflows; today you make one *reliable*, the skill that separates a fragile demo from something you'd put in front of a client. Take your email-triage workflow and harden it against the messiness of real inputs.

**Handle the unhappy paths.** Real automations break on edge cases, not the happy path. Walk through what happens when: the email is empty or just an image; the AI returns malformed JSON; the API call fails or times out; two emails arrive at once. For each, add a defence, an **IF** node that skips empty inputs, a **Code** node wrapped to catch a parse failure, n8n's per-node **"Continue On Fail"** setting so one bad item doesn't kill the whole run. Reliability is just the accumulation of these small guards.

**Error workflows.** n8n lets you attach an **Error Trigger** workflow that fires whenever a workflow fails, so you get a Slack ping instead of silent failure. Set one up now; finding out from your monitoring beats finding out from an angry client (the theme of Week 17, previewed here).

**Test like it'll be abused.** Feed your workflow deliberately awful inputs: blank emails, a 10,000-word email, an email in another language, gibberish. Watch where it breaks and patch it. A workflow that survives your worst test inputs survives production.

**Document the flow.** Add **Sticky Notes** (n8n's annotation feature) explaining what each section does and why. Future-you, and any client who inherits the workflow, will thank you. A documented workflow is a maintainable workflow.

Today: take one workflow and make it bulletproof, guards on empty/malformed inputs, an error-notification path, sticky-note documentation, and a round of hostile testing. Note every failure you found and fixed; that list is proof you build for production, not for the demo.

items.title: Day 7 - No-code automation with n8n
items.body:
## Ship it: a working no-code automation

Wrap Week 2 with a real, runnable n8n automation exported and committed, your first portfolio-grade build.

**What to ship.** Your email-triage (or chosen) workflow, hardened from Day 6, that demonstrates the full pipeline:
- A real **trigger** (Gmail or webhook), not a manual click.
- An **AI step** calling Claude to classify, extract, or draft, with the prompt visible.
- A **transformation** that parses and routes the result.
- An **act** step (draft reply, Slack message, sheet row).
- **Guards** against empty/malformed inputs and an error-notification path.

**How to ship it.** n8n workflows export as JSON (`Download` from the workflow menu). Commit that file plus a short README, what it does, what it triggers on, what it costs per run, and a screenshot of the canvas:

```bash
git add workflows/email-triage.json README.md
git commit -m "Week 2: no-code email-triage automation in n8n (Claude classify + route)"
git push
```

**Why the export matters.** A committed workflow JSON is reproducible, anyone can import it into their n8n and run it, and it's reviewable in version control. That's how you turn "I built a thing" into a portfolio asset and a client deliverable.

You've now built a complete AI automation without writing real code, proof that the highest altitude (no-code) ships fast and is not a lesser path. Next week you drop down a level: Python, for everything n8n can't do gracefully, custom logic, batch processing, and the file-and-data work that needs real code.

weeks.title: Python for automation
weeks.context:
Python is what you reach for when n8n is not flexible enough. Complex data transformations, custom parsing logic, batch processing at scale, and anything requiring code that reads, writes, or manipulates files is faster and more reliable in Python than in a visual workflow builder.

For AI automation, the Python stack is: httpx or requests for API calls, pydantic for structured output validation, python-dotenv for environment management, schedule or APScheduler for cron-like scheduling, and loguru for structured logging. These five libraries cover 80% of automation scripting tasks.

This week you build automation scripts in Python: a script that monitors a folder for new files and processes them through Claude, a batch email processor, and a data extraction script that reads from a CSV and enriches each row with AI-generated content.

items.title: Python basics refresher
items.body:
## Python for automation: the essentials, not the language

You're not here to become a software engineer, you're here to write *automation scripts*: programs that read, transform, call APIs, and write results. That needs a focused slice of Python, and chasing the rest (classes, decorators, async, design patterns) is a distraction that slows you down. Today, lock in the essentials that show up in every automation.

**The five building blocks.** *Variables* hold data (`total = 0`). *Data structures* are the shapes you'll move around constantly: **lists** (`["a","b"]`, ordered collections) and **dicts** (`{"name":"Ada","amount":50}`, the Python form of a JSON object, which is exactly what AI APIs send and receive). *Loops* (`for item in items:`) repeat work over a collection, the heart of batch processing. *Conditionals* (`if amount > 100:`) make decisions. *Functions* (`def process(item):`) name a reusable step so your script reads top-to-bottom like a recipe.

**Dicts and JSON are the same idea.** Almost everything in AI automation is JSON: the data from a webhook, the body you send to Claude, the response you parse. In Python that JSON becomes a **dict**, and `import json` converts between a JSON string and a dict (`json.loads` / `json.dumps`). If you're fluent with dicts, you're fluent with the data of automation.

**Write scripts, not software.** An automation script is often: read input → loop over items → for each, do a transformation or an API call → collect results → write output. Linear, readable, rerunnable. Resist abstracting prematurely; clarity beats cleverness when you (or a client) need to debug it at scale.

**The interpreter and the REPL.** Run scripts with `python script.py`; experiment line-by-line in the REPL or a notebook. The tight "write a line, see what it does" loop is how you learn fastest.

Today: write a small script that defines a list of dicts (fake "orders"), loops over them, and prints each order's total (price × quantity), skipping any with quantity 0. That tiny program is the skeleton of half the automations you'll ever build.

items.title: File automation
items.body:
## File automation: reading, writing, and moving data

A huge share of real automation is just *files*: read a folder of CSVs, rename and sort downloads, combine reports, write results to disk. Python handles all of it cleanly, and these are often the exact tedious tasks businesses pay to eliminate.

**Reading and writing text.** The core idiom uses a context manager so files close themselves: `with open("input.txt") as f: text = f.read()` to read; `with open("out.txt", "w") as f: f.write(result)` to write. The `with` block is the right habit, it prevents the "file left open / locked" bugs that plague beginners.

**Working with the filesystem.** The modern **pathlib** library makes paths sane across operating systems: `from pathlib import Path`; `Path("invoices").glob("*.pdf")` lists every PDF in a folder; `p.name`, `p.stem`, `p.suffix` pick apart a filename. Looping over `glob` results is how you batch-process a folder, the foundation of "process all 200 of these documents."

**CSV, the lingua franca of business data.** `import csv` reads and writes comma-separated files, but for anything analytical, **pandas** (`import pandas as pd`; `pd.read_csv(...)`) is faster to work with: filter, transform, and write back in a few lines. Most "clean up this spreadsheet" jobs are a short pandas script.

**The batch pattern.** Almost every file automation is the same shape: find the files (`glob`) → loop → read each → transform or extract → write the result (or collect into one output). Once you see this pattern, "rename 500 files by their content", "merge a folder of reports", "extract a field from every invoice" all become variations of it.

Today: write a script that finds every `.txt` (or `.csv`) file in a folder, reads each, does a simple transformation (count words, or pull a field), and writes a single summary file with one row per input. You've just automated a real piece of busywork.

days.title: HTTP requests in Python
days.summary: Fetch anything from the internet with one function call.

items.title: HTTP requests in Python
items.body:
## HTTP requests: how your code talks to any API

Every external service, AI models, CRMs, payment systems, data providers, speaks **HTTP**. Learn to make HTTP requests in Python and you can integrate with virtually anything, which is most of what advanced automation is. This is the single most important Python skill for AI automation.

**The library.** Use **httpx** (modern, supports async) or **requests** (simple, ubiquitous). A GET fetches data: `r = httpx.get(url)`; a POST sends data: `r = httpx.post(url, json=payload, headers=headers)`. The response gives you `r.status_code` (did it work?) and `r.json()` (the data, as a dict).

**The anatomy of an API call.** Four parts, every time: the **URL** (which endpoint), the **method** (GET to read, POST to create/act), the **headers** (metadata, crucially your `Authorization` with the API key), and the **body** (the JSON payload you send). When you call Claude next week, it's exactly this, POST to the endpoint, key in the header, prompt in the JSON body. n8n's HTTP Request node was a visual wrapper over precisely this; now you do it in code, with full control.

**Status codes tell you what happened.** `200` success, `4xx` you made a mistake (bad key = `401`, bad request = `400`, too fast = `429`), `5xx` the server failed. *Always check the status* before trusting the body, acting on a failed response's empty data is a classic silent bug.

**Reliability from day one.** Networks fail and APIs rate-limit, so production calls need a **timeout** (`httpx.get(url, timeout=30)`) and **retry-with-backoff** (try again after a pause on `429`/`5xx`). You'll formalise this in Week 17, but build the instinct now: never assume an HTTP call succeeds.

Today: call a free public API (e.g. a JSON test API or a weather endpoint) with httpx, check the status code, parse the JSON, and print one field. Then make it robust, add a timeout and handle a non-200 response gracefully. You now hold the key that unlocks every integration in this course.

items.title: Reading and writing spreadsheets
items.body:
## Spreadsheets in code: the format business runs on

Spreadsheets are where most business data lives, and reading/writing them programmatically is one of the most immediately useful automation skills. "Pull these numbers, transform them, and produce a formatted report every Monday" is a job you can now do in your sleep.

**Excel with openpyxl (and pandas).** **pandas** reads an Excel file into a DataFrame (`pd.read_excel("sales.xlsx")`), where you can filter, group, and compute exactly like a spreadsheet but in repeatable code, then write back with `df.to_excel("out.xlsx")`. When you need *formatting* (bold headers, column widths, formulas, multiple sheets), **openpyxl** gives you cell-level control to produce a polished, client-ready workbook, not just raw data.

**Reading vs producing.** Two distinct jobs. *Reading* is ingestion: get the numbers out of a messy human spreadsheet so your automation can use them. *Producing* is delivery: write a clean, formatted report a human will open. Many automations do both, read a raw export, transform it, and emit a tidy report, and that round-trip is a sellable deliverable on its own.

**The reporting pattern.** A classic automation: on a schedule, read source data (a spreadsheet, a database, an API), compute the summary, and write a formatted Excel (or Google Sheet) report, then email it. You'll wire the pieces together this week; here you're learning the spreadsheet half.

**Watch the data quality.** Real spreadsheets are dirty: merged cells, stray text in number columns, inconsistent dates, blank rows. Reading them robustly means anticipating mess, coerce types, drop junk rows, standardise headers, the same cleaning discipline that makes any data automation trustworthy.

Today: write a script that reads a spreadsheet of sample data, computes a summary (totals per category, say), and writes a *formatted* output workbook with a bold header row and sensible column widths. You've built the core of an automated reporting pipeline.

items.title: Scheduled Python scripts
items.body:
## Scheduled scripts: turning code into an unattended system

A script you have to run by hand is a tool; a script that runs itself on a schedule is an automation. Today you learn the several ways to make Python code run unattended, and, importantly, when to use each.

**In-process scheduling (simplest).** Libraries like **schedule** or **APScheduler** let a long-running Python program trigger functions on a clock: `schedule.every().day.at("08:00").do(run_report)`, then a loop keeps the program alive. Great for development and simple always-on scripts; the catch is the program must stay running, if it crashes or the machine reboots, the schedule dies. Fine for learning, not for production alone.

**OS-level scheduling.** **cron** (Linux/macOS) and **Task Scheduler** (Windows) run a script at set times regardless of whether anything else is running, the OS handles it. `0 8 * * 1-5 python /path/report.py` runs your report at 8 a.m. on weekdays. More robust than in-process because it survives crashes and restarts.

**Cloud scheduling (production).** The real answer for client work: a scheduled job on a server or platform (Railway, Render, a cloud cron, GitHub Actions on a schedule) that runs your containerised script reliably, with logs and alerts. This is Week 16's territory; know now that "where does the schedule live?" is a deployment decision, and your laptop is not the answer for anything a client depends on.

**Design for unattended runs.** Code that no human watches must: **log** what it did (so you can see what happened after the fact), **handle errors** without crashing the whole run (one bad item shouldn't stop the batch), and be **idempotent** (a re-run shouldn't duplicate work). These three habits are what make scheduled automation trustworthy, and they're exactly the production skills of the back half of this course.

Today: take your reporting script and schedule it, locally with `schedule` or via cron/Task Scheduler, to run on an interval. Add basic logging so each run records what it did. Watch it fire on its own. That's the leap from "a script I run" to "a system that runs."

days.title: Day 6 - Python for automation

items.title: Day 6 - Python for automation
items.body:
## Consolidate: combine the pieces into one real script

You've learned files, HTTP, spreadsheets, and scheduling as separate skills. Today you fuse them into a single, complete automation script, the kind you'd actually deploy, because integration is where the real lessons live.

**Build an end-to-end script.** Compose the week's pieces into one workflow, for example: on a schedule, read a folder of new CSV files (files), for each row call an external API to enrich it (HTTP), collect the results, and write a formatted summary report (spreadsheets), logging the whole run. Every skill from the week appears, and you see how they hand off to one another, which is exactly the friction real automation lives in.

**Structure it like a professional.** Split the work into small named functions (`read_inputs()`, `enrich(row)`, `write_report(rows)`) and a `main()` that orchestrates them. Put configuration (paths, API keys via `python-dotenv`) at the top, never hard-code a secret. This structure isn't ceremony, it makes the script testable, readable, and safe to hand to a client.

**Make it survive reality.** Add the production guards you'll formalise later: wrap the per-item work so one failure doesn't abort the batch, check API status codes, time out slow calls, and log each step. Then feed it deliberately broken inputs (a malformed CSV, an API that returns an error) and confirm it degrades gracefully instead of crashing.

**Manage secrets properly.** Use a `.env` file (git-ignored) and `os.environ` / `python-dotenv` to load keys. Committing an API key to GitHub is a real, costly mistake, build the habit of keeping secrets out of code now, before any of it is public.

Today: write one cohesive script that combines files + HTTP + spreadsheet output + scheduling, structured into functions, with secrets in `.env`, logging, and per-item error handling. Run it against messy test data and fix what breaks. This is your first production-shaped Python automation.

items.title: Day 7 - Python for automation
items.body:
## Ship it: a structured Python automation

Wrap Week 3 with a real, committed Python automation, your proof that you can drop below no-code when the job demands it.

**What to ship.** The integrated script from Day 6, polished into a small project:
- A clear entry point (`main.py`) with named functions for each stage (read → process/enrich → write).
- A real combination of skills: file or spreadsheet I/O, at least one HTTP/API call, and a scheduling mechanism (even if just documented cron instructions).
- **Secrets in `.env`** (git-ignored) with a `.env.example` showing the required keys.
- Per-item **error handling** and **logging** so an unattended run is debuggable.
- A `requirements.txt` so anyone can reproduce the environment.

**How to ship it.**

```bash
git add main.py requirements.txt .env.example README.md
git commit -m "Week 3: Python automation (files + API + scheduled report, structured)"
git push
```

The README should state what it does, how to run it, what it needs (keys, inputs), and how it's scheduled.

**Why this matters.** You now span two altitudes: no-code (n8n) for speed, and Python for control. Knowing *which* to reach for, and being fluent in both, is exactly the judgment that makes you employable. Most people know one; you're building both, with the production habits (secrets, logging, error handling) that turn scripts into deliverables.

Next week the two halves meet: you start calling **AI APIs** directly from code, Claude and others, learning structured outputs, tool use, and the techniques that make AI reliable enough to put inside an automation.

weeks.title: Calling AI APIs
weeks.context:
Every major AI model is available via an API. Anthropic (Claude), OpenAI (GPT-4, o1), Google (Gemini), Mistral, Cohere, Together AI, each has a REST API and a Python SDK. This week you learn to call them effectively: structured outputs, tool use / function calling, streaming, and multi-turn conversations.

Structured outputs are how you make AI automation reliable. Instead of asking the model to "return JSON", you define a schema and force the model to return data that matches it. Claude has tool use / JSON mode; OpenAI has structured outputs. When the model is constrained to a schema, parsing errors drop to near zero.

Tool use (also called function calling) is the mechanism that enables agents: you describe a set of tools the model can call (search the web, query a database, send an email), the model decides which tool to call and with what arguments, your code executes the tool, and you return the result to the model. This loop is the foundation of autonomous AI agents.

items.title: Get your API key and make your first call
items.body:
## Your first API call: the model as a function

Until now the AI lived inside n8n's nodes. This week you call it directly from code, which gives you full control over prompts, models, structured outputs, and cost. The mental shift: a language model API is just a *function*, you send a request (model + messages), you get a response (text). Everything else is detail on top of that.

**The Anthropic SDK, the clean path.** Install it (`pip install anthropic`) and the call is short:

```python
from anthropic import Anthropic
client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from your environment
msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarise this in one sentence: ..."}],
)
print(msg.content[0].text)
```

That's the whole pattern: pick a **model**, set a **max_tokens** budget, pass a list of **messages**, read the text off the response. OpenAI's SDK is nearly identical in shape (`client.chat.completions.create`), so learning one teaches you both.

**API key hygiene from the first call.** Your key is a credential that spends real money. Put it in a `.env` file (git-ignored), load it with `python-dotenv`, and never paste it into code you'll commit. A leaked key on GitHub gets scraped and abused within minutes, this habit is non-negotiable.

**The request/response shape.** You send `messages` (a list of role/content turns) and optionally a `system` prompt (instructions that frame the whole interaction). You get back `content` (the model's reply) plus **usage** (input and output token counts, your cost meter). Reading `usage` from day one builds the cost instinct that protects your margins at scale.

**Model tiers and the cost-quality trade.** The current Claude family spans tiers: **Opus** (claude-opus-4-8) for the hardest reasoning, **Sonnet** (claude-sonnet-4-6) for the everyday workhorse balance, **Haiku** (claude-haiku-4-5) for cheap, fast, high-volume steps. Default to Sonnet; reach up to Opus only when a task genuinely needs it, and down to Haiku for simple classification at scale. Model choice is a cost decision you'll make on every automation.

Today: get an API key, store it in `.env`, and make your first call from Python, ask Claude to summarise a paragraph. Print the response *and* the token usage. You've just turned the model into a function you can build with.

days.title: Text summarisation

items.title: Text summarisation
items.body:
## Summarisation: the first reliable building block

Summarisation is the simplest high-value AI task and a perfect place to learn to control a model's output. "Turn this long thing into a short useful thing" appears everywhere, email digests, meeting notes, report condensing, and getting it *reliable* teaches habits you'll reuse for every task.

**Control the output, don't hope for it.** A vague "summarise this" gives unpredictable length and style, useless in automation where the next step expects a known shape. Specify everything: "Summarise the text below in **exactly three bullet points**, each under 15 words, focusing on **decisions and action items**. Return only the bullets, no preamble." The more you constrain length, focus, and format, the more consistent the output across thousands of runs.

**System vs user prompt.** Put *role and rules* in the **system** prompt ("You are a precise summariser. You never add information not in the source.") and the *content to act on* in the **user** message. This separation makes prompts reusable, the system prompt is your fixed policy, the user message is the variable input.

**Guard against the failure modes.** Summarisers have two classic risks: **hallucination** (inventing facts not in the source, deadly for anything factual) and **length drift** (ignoring your limit on long inputs). Mitigate by instructing "use only information present in the text" and by validating the output (e.g. check it's actually three bullets) before trusting it downstream.

**Mind the context window and cost.** Very long inputs cost more and may exceed limits, you'll learn chunking in Week 8. For now, note that input length drives token cost, so summarising is also a cost-management skill: a cheap Haiku call may summarise perfectly well where Opus would be overkill.

Today: build a `summarise(text)` function that takes any text and returns a structured three-bullet summary, with a system prompt enforcing "facts only" and length limits. Test it on a long article and a short note; confirm it holds format on both. That's your first reusable, reliable AI building block.

items.title: Text classification
items.body:
## Classification: the workhorse of automation

Classification, "which category does this belong to?", is the single most common AI step in real automations: route this email, tag this ticket, flag this transaction, sort this document. It's also where *structured, constrained output* matters most, because the next step branches on the answer.

**Constrain to a fixed set.** The cardinal rule: tell the model the *exact* allowed labels and forbid anything else. "Classify the message into **exactly one** of: `billing`, `technical`, `sales`, `other`. Respond with only the label." Without this, the model invents new categories ("billing-related?") that break your routing logic. A closed label set is what makes classification automatable.

**Return structured data, not prose.** For anything beyond a single label, ask for JSON: `{"category": "billing", "confidence": "high", "reason": "mentions an invoice"}`. Structured output means the next node can act programmatically, no fragile text-parsing. You'll make this bulletproof with tool use tomorrow; today, ask for JSON and parse it.

**Confidence and the escape hatch.** Real classification needs a "not sure" path. Add an `uncertain` label or a confidence field, and route low-confidence items to a human. An automation that *knows when it doesn't know* is far safer than one that confidently miscategorises, this single design choice prevents most embarrassing failures.

**Cheap model, big volume.** Classification is usually simple enough for the **Haiku** tier, fast and cheap, which matters because you may run it on thousands of items a day. Don't pay Opus prices to sort emails. Match the model to the difficulty.

**Few-shot when categories are subtle.** If labels are ambiguous, show 2–3 labelled examples in the prompt ("Example: 'my card was declined' → billing"). Examples pin down your intended boundaries better than any description, you'll go deeper on this in Week 5.

Today: build a `classify(text)` function returning `{category, confidence}` over a fixed label set, with an `uncertain` fallback. Test it on 10 varied inputs, including ambiguous ones, and confirm the uncertain ones get flagged rather than guessed. That's production-grade routing.

days.title: Q&A over a document

items.title: Q&A over a document
items.body:
## Q&A over a document: grounding the model in your data

"Answer questions about *this specific document*" is a foundational pattern, the seed of every support bot, contract assistant, and knowledge tool. The key idea: you **ground** the model by putting the relevant source text *in the prompt*, so it answers from your data, not its training memory.

**The pattern: stuff the context.** For a document that fits the model's context window, the approach is simple: include the document in the prompt and ask your question. "Using **only** the document below, answer the question. If the answer isn't in the document, say 'not found'. \n\nDOCUMENT:\n{text}\n\nQUESTION: {question}". The model reads the provided text and answers from it. This is "RAG without the retrieval", and it's the right tool whenever your source fits in context.

**The anti-hallucination instruction is everything.** The phrase "**use only the document; if it's not there, say so**" is what separates a trustworthy Q&A system from one that confidently makes things up. Without it, the model fills gaps with plausible-but-wrong answers drawn from its training. With it, you get honest "not found", which is exactly what a business needs.

**When the document doesn't fit.** Long documents exceed the context window. Two paths: **chunk** the document and answer over the relevant pieces (Week 8), or, for a *large knowledge base*, retrieve only the relevant chunks first, that's **RAG**, the major topic of Week 14. Today's in-context approach is the foundation both build on; understanding it makes RAG obvious later.

**Citations build trust.** Ask the model to quote the supporting sentence ("answer, then quote the exact text you used"). Citations let a human verify, and verifiable answers are what make AI usable in serious settings.

Today: build an `ask(document, question)` function that answers strictly from a provided document, returns "not found" when the answer is absent, and quotes its supporting sentence. Test it with a question that *is* answered and one that *isn't*, the second test, getting an honest "not found", is the one that proves your system is trustworthy.

[CODE] Create triage.py:

from openai import OpenAI
from dotenv import load_dotenv
import os

load_dotenv()
client = OpenAI(api_key=os.getenv('OPENAI_API_KEY'))

def classify(text):
 r = client.chat.completions.create(
 model='gpt-4o-mini',
 messages=[{'role':'system','content':'Reply with one word: URGENT, NORMAL, or LOW.'},{'role':'user','content':text}]
 )
 return r.choices[0].message.content.strip()

def summarise(text):
 r = client.chat.completions.create(
 model='gpt-4o-mini',
 messages=[{'role':'system','content':'Summarise in one sentence.'},{'role':'user','content':text}]
 )
 return r.choices[0].message.content.strip()

message = 'Our main database crashed an hour ago. Customers cannot place orders. The engineering team has been paged but no fix yet. This is costing us $500/minute.'

summary = summarise(message)

items.title: Day 6 - Calling AI APIs
items.body:
## Consolidate: a reliable, cost-aware API module

You can make individual calls; today you turn them into a small, reusable **module** you'd actually drop into client projects, the difference between scattered scripts and a professional toolkit.

**Wrap the model behind your own function.** Build a thin layer, e.g. `ai.py` with `summarise()`, `classify()`, and `extract()`, each calling the model with a tested prompt and returning *validated* structured data. The rest of your code calls *your* functions, not the raw SDK. This means a prompt fix or a model swap happens in one place, and your business logic stays clean. It also lets you switch providers (Claude ↔ another) behind a stable interface.

**Build in reliability.** Production API code needs: **retries with backoff** on rate limits (`429`) and transient `5xx` errors; **timeouts** so a hung call doesn't freeze the pipeline; and **graceful degradation** (return a clear error or an `uncertain` result rather than crashing). Wrap every call so one failure is handled, not fatal, this is what survives real traffic.

**Track cost.** Read `usage` (input/output tokens) off each response and log it. Knowing your per-run token cost lets you price client work and spot when a prompt has bloated. At scale, a 2× longer prompt is a 2× bigger bill, observability here is margin protection.

**Choose models deliberately.** In your module, default each function to the *cheapest tier that does the job*: Haiku for classification, Sonnet for summarisation and extraction, Opus reserved for genuinely hard reasoning. Make the model a parameter so you can tune cost per task without rewriting logic.

Today: package your week's calls into a small `ai` module with validated outputs, retry/timeout handling, token-cost logging, and sensible per-task model defaults. Then run a batch through it and read off the total token cost. You now have a reusable, production-shaped AI layer, not just example snippets.

weeks.title: Prompt engineering for automation
weeks.context:
Prompt engineering for automation is different from prompt engineering for chat. In a chat context, you iterate in real time and adjust. In automation, the prompt runs thousands of times without you watching. A prompt that works 95% of the time has a 5% failure rate, at 1,000 runs per day, that is 50 failures per day.

Reliability is the primary metric for automation prompts. A prompt that extracts data correctly 95% of the time at scale is worse than a prompt that achieves 99.9%, because at scale, 5% failures are operational incidents. This week you learn the techniques that move prompts from "usually works" to "always works": few-shot examples, explicit output constraints, chain-of-thought for complex tasks, and systematic prompt testing.

You also learn to write system prompts that are robust: they define the task, the constraints, the output format, how to handle uncertainty, and what to do when the input is ambiguous or missing required information.

days.title: System vs user prompts
days.summary: The system prompt is your instruction manual. The user prompt is the input.

items.title: System vs user prompts
items.body:
## System vs user prompts: separating policy from input

Prompt engineering for *automation* is a different discipline from prompting in a chat. In chat you watch each reply and adjust; in automation the prompt runs thousands of times unattended, so it must be *reliable by construction*. The foundation of that reliability is structuring your prompt correctly, starting with the system/user split.

**The two roles, and why they matter.** The **system prompt** sets fixed policy: who the model is, the rules it always follows, the output format it must produce. The **user message** carries the variable input the policy is applied to. "You are a precise invoice extractor. Always return JSON matching the schema. Never guess missing fields, use null." (system) vs. the actual invoice text (user). Keeping rules in the system prompt means they apply identically across every run, while only the input changes.

**Why the split improves reliability.** Models weight system instructions as persistent constraints, so your formatting and safety rules hold more consistently when they live there rather than being repeated in each user message. It also keeps your code clean: one fixed system prompt, a stream of varying user inputs, exactly the shape of an automation.

**Be explicit and exhaustive in the system prompt.** Unlike chat, you can't clarify mid-run. Spell out the role, the allowed outputs, the format, the edge-case behaviour ("if the text is empty, return `{}`"), and what *not* to do ("never add commentary"). Every ambiguity you leave is a failure mode that will surface somewhere in 1,000 runs.

**Treat prompts as versioned code.** A prompt is logic. Store it in your repo, version it, and note why you changed it, because a "small tweak" can shift behaviour across thousands of runs. Prompt changes deserve the same care as code changes.

Today: take one task from last week and rewrite its prompt with a clean system/user split, putting *all* rules and format requirements in an exhaustive system prompt and only the variable input in the user message. Run it on several inputs and confirm the format holds identically each time. That consistency is what automation demands.

items.title: Output formatting, make AI return structured data
items.body:
## Forcing structure: make output safe for code to consume

In automation, the model's output is *input to your next step*, so it must be a shape your code can rely on, every time. Free-form prose is unusable; structured, schema-conformant output is the whole game. Today you make structure non-negotiable.

**Tool use is the strongest guarantee.** As in Week 4, defining a tool with a JSON `input_schema` forces the model to return arguments matching that schema, no preamble, no markdown fences, no "Sure! Here's your JSON". For automation, prefer tool use (or a provider's structured-output mode) over "please return JSON" whenever you can, because *prompted* JSON occasionally drifts and *enforced* JSON does not. The schema is a contract the model must honour.

**When you must parse text, parse defensively.** Sometimes you only have prompted JSON. Then: instruct "return only valid JSON, no other text", strip stray markdown fences, and wrap `json.loads` in error handling that retries or flags the item instead of crashing. Never assume the model's text is clean, validate it at the boundary.

**Validate with a schema, always.** Even enforced output should pass through **pydantic** (or equivalent) so types, enums, and required fields are checked before you act. A `confidence` that should be `high/medium/low` arriving as `"pretty sure"` must be caught *here*, not three steps later when it corrupts a database write. Validation turns "probably fine" into "provably fine".

**Design schemas for failure, not just success.** Include fields that let the model express uncertainty or absence: `null` for missing data, an `uncertain` enum value, a `notes` field for ambiguity. A schema that only models the happy path forces the model to fabricate; one that allows "I don't know" gets you honest, safe output.

Today: convert one task to **enforced** structured output via tool use, define the schema (including null/uncertain options), and validate every result with pydantic before acting. Feed it a malformed or incomplete input and confirm your validation catches it cleanly. Structure plus validation is the bedrock of reliable automation.

days.summary: Show the AI examples of what you want, it learns instantly.

items.title: Few-shot prompting
items.body:
## Few-shot prompting: teaching by example

When a task is subtle, edge cases, a specific format, a judgment boundary, describing the rules in words only goes so far. **Few-shot prompting** (showing the model a handful of input→output examples) is often the single most effective way to lock in reliable behaviour, because examples communicate what descriptions can't.

**Why examples beat description.** "Classify sentiment" is ambiguous, where does a lukewarm review fall? But three labelled examples ("'It's fine, I guess' → neutral") pin the boundary precisely. Examples encode the exact format, tone, and edge-case handling you want, and the model pattern-matches to them. For automation, where consistency is everything, a few good examples can lift a flaky prompt to near-perfect.

**Choose examples deliberately.** Pick examples that cover the *hard* and *boundary* cases, not the obvious ones, the ambiguous input, the tricky format, the "this should be uncertain" case. Include a tricky negative ("this looks like X but is actually Y"). Two or three well-chosen examples usually beat ten random ones; they teach the decision, not just the task.

**Format examples exactly like real output.** Show the input and the *exact* structured output you expect (the same JSON shape). The model mirrors the format it sees, so consistent examples produce consistent output. Inconsistent examples teach inconsistency.

**Few-shot has a cost.** Every example is tokens on *every* run, so balance reliability against cost. If a task is simple, zero-shot with a clear schema is cheaper. If it's subtle and high-volume, the few-shot tokens are worth it for the error reduction. This trade, accuracy vs token cost, is a recurring automation decision.

Today: take your least-reliable prompt from this week and add 2–3 carefully chosen few-shot examples covering its hardest edge cases. Measure before/after on a test set of tricky inputs and note the improvement and the added token cost. You've just learned the highest-leverage reliability technique in prompt engineering.

items.title: Prompt templates
items.body:
## Prompt templates: reusable, parameterised, versioned

In automation a prompt isn't a one-off message, it's a **template** filled with different data on every run. Treating prompts as parameterised, versioned templates (not strings scattered through your code) is what makes an automation maintainable and your prompt-improvements safe.

**Separate template from data.** A template has fixed instructions and **placeholders** for the variable parts: "Extract the {fields} from the document below. Return JSON. \n\n{document}". Your code fills the placeholders per run. Keep templates out of business logic, in their own files or a prompts module, so you can read, edit, and review them without touching code.

**Build a small template system.** Even simple Python `str.format` or a light templating tool works. The goal: one named template per task, loaded and filled by your `ai` module. When a prompt needs improvement, you edit *one* template and every call benefits, no hunting through the codebase for inline strings.

**Inject data safely.** Two real risks when stuffing user data into a prompt. **Delimiting**: clearly fence the variable input ("DOCUMENT: \n```\n{document}\n```") so the model can tell instructions from content. **Prompt injection**: untrusted input may contain text like "ignore previous instructions and..." Treat external data as hostile, keep authoritative instructions in the system prompt, fence user content, and never let injected text override your rules. This matters the moment your automation touches emails, web pages, or user uploads.

**Version and test templates.** Store templates in git with a version note. Before deploying a prompt change, run it against a saved set of test inputs and compare outputs, a "prompt regression test". A prompt edit that fixes one case can silently break three others; a test set catches that before production does.

Today: refactor your week's prompts into named, parameterised templates in a `prompts/` module, with fenced data injection and a small saved test set you can re-run after any edit. You've turned ad-hoc prompts into maintainable, reviewable assets.
