items.title: AI data analysis on spreadsheet data
items.body:
## AI over your data: natural-language analysis and text-to-SQL

Now connect the *intelligence* to the *data*. Two of the most valuable enterprise patterns live here: letting AI **analyse** spreadsheet/database data in natural language, and **text-to-SQL**, turning a business person's plain-English question into a real query. Both put answers in the hands of people who can't write SQL.

**AI data analysis on tabular data.** Give the model your data (or a representative sample/summary) and ask analytical questions: "what are the top 3 drivers of the cost increase?", "summarise the trends in this sales data", "flag any anomalies". For small data, include it in the prompt; for larger data, compute summaries/aggregates with pandas first and feed *those* to the model (cheaper, and avoids dumping huge tables into context). The model adds the *interpretation* layer on top of your computation, exactly the "so what" that turns numbers into decisions.

**Text-to-SQL: the high-value enterprise pattern.** Instead of an analyst writing SQL for every ad-hoc question, you build a system where a business user asks in English ("how many orders shipped late last month?") and the model generates the SQL, which you run against the database and return the answer. The model needs the **schema** (table and column names, types, relationships) in its prompt to generate correct queries, schema-in, SQL-out. Done well, this is a force-multiplier that frees analysts from endless one-off query requests.

**Text-to-SQL safety, this is critical.** Executing model-generated SQL on a real database is *dangerous* if naive. Guardrails are mandatory: connect with a **read-only** user (so a hallucinated `DROP TABLE` can't fire), **validate** the generated SQL (allow only `SELECT`, reject anything else), use a **sandbox/limited** database where possible, and add `LIMIT`s to prevent runaway queries. Never run raw AI-generated SQL with write access against production. The pattern is powerful *only* when bounded; unbounded, it's a disaster waiting to happen.

**Verify the answer.** Generated SQL can be subtly wrong (wrong join, wrong filter) and return a confident-but-incorrect number. Show the generated query alongside the answer so a user can sanity-check it, and validate results where you can. Transparency (here's the question, here's the SQL, here's the result) is what makes text-to-SQL trustworthy.

Today: build a small text-to-SQL helper over a sample SQLite database, schema in the prompt, model generates a `SELECT`, you validate it's read-only, run it, and return the answer *with* the query shown. Test it with a few plain-English questions, including one that should be rejected (a non-SELECT). Safe, transparent, useful, that's the pattern.

## Build it: the automation you scoped in Week 1

Today is a milestone: you build the real automation you scoped back in **Week 1**. You now have every skill it needs, triggers, AI calls, structured output, reliability, data persistence, delivery, and this is where it all converges into the working system you set out to create.

**Revisit and refine your Week 1 brief.** Reread the brief you committed in Week 1: the trigger, input, the one-sentence AI judgment, output/act, and who benefits. With ten weeks of skills, you can now see it clearly, and probably improve it. Refine the scope to what you can build *well* now: a sharp, finished automation beats an ambitious half-built one (the same scoping discipline that finishes projects).

**Map the brief onto your toolkit.** Walk the pipeline and assign each piece to a skill you've learned: the **trigger** (schedule/webhook/email, Weeks 2–3, 9), the **fetch** (file/PDF/web/Sheet/API, Weeks 3, 7, 8, 10), the **AI judgment** (your reliable `ai` module with structured output, Weeks 4–5), the **state** (SQLite, today), the **act/delivery** (Sheet/Excel/email/Slack, Weeks 9–10). Seeing your own brief decompose cleanly into learned skills is the moment the course pays off.

**Build the spine first, then harden.** Get the happy path working end-to-end before polishing, prove the core flow runs and produces the right output on a clean input. *Then* add the reliability layer (validation, error isolation, retries, logging, idempotency) and the safety guards (human-in-the-loop where actions are consequential). Spine first, robustness second, mirrors how you'll build for clients.

**Build against real data and a real beneficiary.** Use actual data (or a faithful sample) and keep the real beneficiary in mind, the person whose time this saves. An automation built against reality surfaces the real edge cases; one built against imagined inputs breaks on contact with the world. If you can, show an early version to that person and watch them use it.

Today: build the core, working version of your Week 1 automation end-to-end, real trigger, real AI step with reliable structured output, persistent state, real output/delivery. Get it producing correct results on real data. Note what's still rough; you'll harden it as the course continues. The thing you imagined in Week 1 now runs.

items.title: Day 6 - Database and spreadsheet automation
items.body:
## Consolidate: connect the data layer end-to-end

Today you solidify the data backbone of your automations, making sure intelligence, persistence, and delivery work together cleanly, because in production, the data plumbing is where reliability is won or lost.

**Unify the data flow.** A mature automation has a clear data path: inputs come from somewhere (Sheet, database, API, files), get processed (AI + logic), state is tracked (database), and outputs go somewhere (report, Sheet, notification). Lay yours out explicitly and check each hand-off: Is the source read reliably? Is state updated atomically (so a crash mid-run doesn't corrupt it)? Are outputs written transactionally (no half-written report)? Clean hand-offs are what let an automation run unattended for months.

**Make persistence robust.** Your database/state layer needs care: use parameterised queries (no injection), handle the "already exists" / "not found" cases, and design for idempotency so a re-run reconciles rather than duplicates. Add a simple audit log table, every run records what it did, which is gold when a client asks "what happened on the 14th?" or when you're debugging.

**Validate data at every boundary.** Data from a Sheet a human edits, or an API, or AI generation, is untrusted: types drift, fields go missing, values go out of range. Validate on the way in (coerce types, check required fields) and on the way out (sanity-check computed results before writing/delivering). The bad-data-in, confident-wrong-output-out failure is silent and costly; boundary validation catches it.

**Reporting and observability as data, too.** Your automation should produce not just business output but operational data: how many items processed, how many succeeded/failed/escalated, total cost. Store these and surface them (a summary row, a Slack message). This previews Week 17's monitoring, an automation that reports on its own health is one you can trust and a client can see working.

Today: harden the data layer of your main automation, robust persistence with an audit log, boundary validation on inputs and outputs, and a per-run operational summary (counts, cost, failures). Run it a few times, including with deliberately messy input, and confirm the state stays consistent and the run summary tells you exactly what happened.

items.title: Day 7 - Database and spreadsheet automation
items.body:
## Ship it: a data-connected automation

Wrap Week 10 by shipping the real automation you scoped in Week 1, now data-connected, persistent, and delivering results, plus the data skills that power it.

**What to ship.**
- Your **Week 1 automation**, working end-to-end on real data: trigger → fetch → reliable AI step → persistent state → output/delivery.
- A **persistence layer** (SQLite or a Sheet) providing memory, deduplication, status tracking, and an audit log, idempotent across re-runs.
- **Data integration**: reading from and/or writing to spreadsheets/Sheets/databases, and (if relevant) a *safe* text-to-SQL or AI-analysis component (read-only, validated).
- **Formatted delivery** (Excel/Sheet report, email, or notification) and a per-run operational summary.

**How to ship it.**

```bash
git add automation/ README.md
git commit -m "Week 10: data-connected automation (the Week 1 build) - persistence, reporting, safe text-to-SQL"
git push
```

The README should describe what the automation does, who it serves, its data flow, and its reliability/safety measures, written so the *beneficiary* could understand it.

**Why this matters.** You've reached the course's first summit: the automation you imagined in Week 1 is *real and running*, built from skills you now own. It connects triggers, AI judgment, persistent memory, and delivery, the full shape of a production automation. That's a portfolio centrepiece and proof you can take an idea from brief to working system.

The first half built *capabilities*; the second half builds *sophistication and business*. Next week begins the agent-building phase with **LangChain**, the framework that turns the patterns you implemented by hand into composable, production-ready building blocks, so you can build more complex systems faster.

weeks.title: LangChain basics
weeks.context:
LangChain is a framework for building LLM-powered applications. It provides abstractions for the most common patterns: chains (sequences of LLM calls), agents (LLMs with tools), memory (persisting conversation state), and document loaders + retrievers (for RAG). The value of LangChain is reducing boilerplate, the same patterns you would implement manually in 200 lines take 20 lines with LangChain.

The critique of LangChain is equally valid: it adds abstraction and magic that makes debugging harder, and its API surface changes frequently. For production systems, many teams drop LangChain and implement the specific patterns they need directly. You should know both approaches: LangChain for rapid prototyping and experimentation, direct API calls for production.

This week you use LangChain to build the same automations you built in Python in previous weeks, compare the implementation and form your own opinion.

items.title: Install LangChain and make your first chain
items.body:
## LangChain: less boilerplate, same patterns

For ten weeks you built the patterns of AI automation by hand, calls, structured output, tool loops, agents. **LangChain** is a framework that packages those exact patterns into reusable building blocks, so what took 200 lines takes 20. Crucially, you're learning it *after* building from first principles, which means you'll understand what it's doing under the hood and can debug it when it misbehaves, an edge most LangChain users don't have.

**What LangChain gives you.** Abstractions for the common patterns: **chains** (sequences of LLM calls and logic), **agents** (LLMs with tools, the loop you hand-built), **memory** (persisting conversation state), **output parsers** (structured output), and **document loaders + retrievers** (the foundation of RAG, Week 14). Its value is *reducing boilerplate* and giving you a consistent, composable interface across providers and patterns. It's the difference between assembling a system from tested components versus wiring everything from scratch each time.

**The core idea: composable components.** LangChain's modern interface (LCEL, the LangChain Expression Language) lets you *compose* components with a pipe-like syntax: a prompt template → a model → an output parser, chained together as one runnable unit. Each piece is swappable (change the model without touching the rest), and the composition is the "chain". This composability is what makes building complex pipelines manageable.

**A first chain.** Install (`pip install langchain langchain-anthropic`), then the minimal chain is: a **prompt template** (with placeholders) → a **chat model** (e.g. Claude via `langchain-anthropic`) → an **output parser** (e.g. to a string or structured object). You invoke it with your inputs and get the parsed result. That's the unit you'll compose everything from.

**Use it judiciously.** LangChain is powerful but adds abstraction, and abstraction can obscure what's happening (and occasionally fight you). The pro move: use it where it genuinely saves work (agents, RAG, complex chains), but don't be afraid to drop to direct API calls (your Week 4 skills) when a task is simple. Framework when it helps, first principles when it's clearer.

Today: install LangChain, set up Claude as the model, and build your first chain, a prompt template → model → output parser, then invoke it on a few inputs. Compare it to the equivalent direct API call you wrote in Week 4. Seeing the same result with less boilerplate, while understanding both, is the point.

days.title: Output parsers

items.title: Output parsers
items.body:
## Output parsers: structured results, the LangChain way

You already know structured output is the backbone of reliable automation. LangChain's **output parsers** are its tools for getting it, turning the model's response into clean, typed Python objects, and they integrate neatly with the tool-use and pydantic skills you already have.

**What output parsers do.** A parser sits at the end of a chain and converts the model's raw text into a usable structure: a string, a list, JSON, or, most powerfully, a **pydantic object**. The `PydanticOutputParser` (or structured-output helpers) takes a pydantic schema, injects formatting instructions into the prompt telling the model what shape to return, and parses + validates the response into that typed object. It's your Week 4–5 pattern (schema + validation) wrapped into a reusable component.

**Schema-driven, like before.** You define the output shape as a pydantic model (fields, types, descriptions), and the parser handles both directions: instructing the model to produce it, and validating what comes back. This is the same "define the contract, enforce the contract" discipline, now declarative. The field descriptions in your schema double as guidance to the model, write them well.

**Modern structured output.** LangChain also exposes models' native structured-output / tool-use capabilities directly (e.g. `model.with_structured_output(MySchema)`), which is the most reliable path because it uses the provider's *enforced* structured output (Claude's tool use) rather than prompt-and-parse. Prefer this when available, it's the framework wrapper over the guaranteed-structure technique you learned in Week 4.

**Handle parse failures.** Even with parsers, validation can fail on a stubborn malformed response. LangChain offers retrying/fixing parsers that re-prompt the model to correct its output, the framework version of your validate-and-retry pattern. Always have a failure path; structured output is *more* reliable, not infallible.

Today: build a chain that returns a validated **pydantic object** via an output parser (or `with_structured_output`), e.g. extract `{name, category, priority}` from text. Feed it varied inputs and confirm you get clean, typed objects, and that a malformed case is caught or retried. You've got the LangChain idiom for the structured output your automations live on.

days.title: Memory, giving your chain a short-term memory
days.summary: Maintain conversation history across multiple turns.

items.title: Memory, giving your chain a short-term memory
items.body:
## Memory: giving a chain short-term recall

A single chain call is stateless, it has no idea what was said before. **Memory** is how LangChain lets a chain *remember* across turns, which is essential for anything conversational (a chatbot, a multi-turn assistant) and useful for agents that accumulate context. Understanding memory also clarifies a key constraint: models have no inherent memory; *you* supply it.

**The fundamental truth: the model is stateless.** Every API call is independent, the model only knows what's in *this* request. "Memory" is an illusion you create by *including previous messages in the next prompt*. LangChain's memory components automate this: they store the conversation history and automatically inject it into each new call, so the chain appears to remember. Internally it's just "keep the message history and resend the relevant part", exactly what you'd do by hand.

**Types of memory, and the trade-off.** The simplest is **buffer memory**: keep the full conversation and resend it every turn, accurate but grows without bound, eventually blowing the context window and the cost budget. **Windowed memory** keeps only the last N turns (bounded, but forgets older context). **Summary memory** periodically summarises old turns into a compact note (preserves gist, costs an extra call). The choice is a classic engineering trade between completeness, cost, and context limits, the same tension you'll manage in long-running agents.

**Why this matters for automation.** Most *automations* are actually stateless-by-design (process each item independently), and that's good, simpler and cheaper. Memory matters specifically when context must persist: a support chatbot remembering the conversation, an agent accumulating findings across many tool calls, a multi-turn intake assistant. Use memory where genuine continuity is needed, not by default.

**Persistence beyond a session.** In-memory memory vanishes when the process ends. For automations that need to remember across runs or sessions (a chatbot that recalls a returning user), back memory with a real store, your SQLite skills from Week 10, or a vector store for semantic recall (Week 14). LangChain supports pluggable persistent memory backends.

Today: build a conversational chain *with* memory and have a short multi-turn exchange where it correctly references something said earlier (e.g. you tell it your name, then later ask it). Then swap buffer memory for windowed or summary memory and observe the difference. You now understand that memory is just managed message history, and how to bound it.

items.title: Chain with conversation memory
items.body:
[CODE] Create memory_chain.py:

from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
from langchain_core.chat_history import InMemoryChatMessageHistory
from langchain_core.runnables.history import RunnableWithMessageHistory
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate, MessagesPlaceholder
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()

llm = ChatOpenAI(model='gpt-4o-mini')

prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([
 ('system', 'You are a helpful assistant.'),
 MessagesPlaceholder('history'),
 ('human', '{input}')
])

store = {}
def get_history(session_id):
 if session_id not in store:
 store[session_id] = InMemoryChatMessageHistory()
 return store[session_id]

chain = RunnableWithMessageHistory(prompt | llm, get_history, input_messages_key='input', history_messages_key='history')

config = {'configurable': {'session_id': 'user1'}}
print(chain.invoke({'input': 'My name is Abdoulie'}, config=config).content)
print(chain.invoke({'input': 'What is my name?'}, config=config).content) # remembers

items.title: LangChain tools
items.body:
## LangChain tools: agents, the framework way

In Week 6 you hand-built tools and the agent loop. LangChain packages all of that, **tools**, the agent executor, the ReAct loop, into ready components, so you can build capable agents quickly while standing on the understanding you already have.

**Defining a tool.** A LangChain tool wraps a Python function with a name, a description, and an argument schema, the exact same three things you defined by hand. The cleanest modern way is the `@tool` decorator on a typed function with a good docstring: a `@tool`-decorated `search_web(query: str)` whose docstring is "Search the web for current information." LangChain reads the signature and docstring to build the schema and description the model sees. Your Week 6 lesson holds: the **description is the interface**, write it so the model knows exactly when and how to use the tool.

**Wiring tools into an agent.** Give a model a list of tools and an agent executor, and LangChain runs the loop you built by hand: the model reasons, requests a tool, the executor runs it, feeds the result back, and repeats until done. What was ~100 lines of loop-and-message-management is now a few lines, but because you built it yourself, you know exactly what's happening inside and can debug it when the agent loops, picks the wrong tool, or misbehaves.

**The same guardrails still apply, and are still yours to add.** Frameworks don't remove the need for guardrails, they just give you places to put them. You still set a **max-iteration** limit, **validate** tool arguments for consequential actions, handle tool **failures** (return errors to the model so it adapts), and watch **cost** (each iteration is a call). A LangChain agent without these is exactly as dangerous as a hand-built one without them.

**Built-in tools and integrations.** LangChain ships many pre-built tools and integrations (web search, Wikipedia, calculators, API wrappers, database tools), so you often don't write the tool at all. Useful, but vet them: know what each actually does and its cost/limits before trusting an agent with it.

Today: rebuild your Week 6 agent in LangChain, define 2–3 tools with the `@tool` decorator, wire them into an agent executor with a max-iteration cap, and run it on a task. Compare it to your hand-built version: far less code, same behaviour, and you understand every step. That combination, leverage *plus* understanding, is exactly where you want to be.

from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
from langchain_core.tools import tool
from langchain.agents import create_tool_calling_agent, AgentExecutor

from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()

@tool
def get_word_count(text: str) -> int:
 '''Count the number of words in a text.'''

@tool
def reverse_text(text: str) -> str:
 '''Reverse a string of text.'''

llm = ChatOpenAI(model='gpt-4o-mini')

 ('system', 'You are a helpful assistant with tools.'),

])

executor = AgentExecutor(agent=agent, tools=tools, verbose=True)

result = executor.invoke({'input': 'How many words are in the phrase hello world today?'})
print(result['output'])

days.title: Sequential chains, multi-step pipelines
days.summary: Chain multiple LLM calls where output of one feeds the next.

items.title: Sequential chains, multi-step pipelines
items.body:
## Sequential chains: composing multi-step pipelines

Not every multi-step task needs a full agent. When the steps are *known in advance*, a **sequential chain**, a fixed pipeline where each step's output feeds the next, is simpler, cheaper, more predictable, and easier to debug than an agent. Knowing when to use a chain vs an agent is a key design judgment.

**Chains vs agents, the core distinction.** An **agent** *decides* its steps dynamically (flexible, but less predictable and more expensive). A **chain** runs a *fixed* sequence you defined (predictable, cheap, debuggable). If you know the steps, "extract data → validate → summarise → format report", use a chain. Reserve agents for when the path genuinely can't be predetermined (open-ended research, variable tasks). Many problems people reach for agents on are really just chains; choosing the chain is often the more professional call.

**Building sequential chains.** With LCEL you compose steps with the pipe syntax: the output of one runnable flows into the next. A step can be an LLM call, a data transformation (plain Python), a parser, or another chain. You build a pipeline like `extract | validate | summarise | format`, each stage focused and testable. Composing focused stages beats one giant prompt, each is debuggable and swappable, the same "small composable steps" principle from your hand-built pipelines.

**Branching and routing.** Real pipelines aren't always linear. LangChain supports **conditional routing** (send the data down different sub-chains based on a value, e.g. route by document type) and combining results. This lets a chain handle variation without becoming an agent, you encode the *known* decision logic explicitly rather than delegating it to the model. Explicit routing is more reliable than agent improvisation when the branches are known.

**Debuggability is the payoff.** Because a chain's steps are fixed and explicit, when something goes wrong you can inspect each stage's input and output and pinpoint the failure, far easier than debugging an agent's emergent behaviour. For production automations, this predictability is often worth more than an agent's flexibility. Use **LangSmith** (LangChain's tracing tool) to see every step's I/O when debugging.

Today: build a sequential chain for a real multi-step task (e.g. extract → validate → summarise → format), composing focused stages with LCEL, and add one conditional branch (route by some value). Run it and trace each stage's I/O. Then articulate, in a sentence, why this task is better as a chain than an agent. That judgment is the lesson.

])

])

items.title: Day 6 - LangChain basics
items.body:
## Consolidate: chain vs agent, and clean composition

Today you cement the central design judgment of agent-building, *chain or agent?*, and practise composing LangChain components into clean, debuggable systems, because the framework's power is wasted if you reach for the wrong pattern.

**Internalise the decision.** For a given task, ask: *do I know the steps in advance?* If yes → **chain** (fixed, cheap, predictable, debuggable). If the path depends on what's discovered along the way → **agent** (flexible, costlier, less predictable). And often the best answer is *hybrid*: a chain that calls an agent for one genuinely-open sub-step, or an agent whose tools are themselves chains. Most robust production systems lean toward chains with agents used surgically, not agents everywhere. Sketch two of your own use cases and classify each.

**Compose cleanly.** Practise building systems as compositions of small, named, testable components, prompt templates, parsers, tools, sub-chains, rather than monolithic blobs. Each component should do one thing and be independently testable. Clean composition is what lets you build complex automations without them becoming unmaintainable, and what lets you swap a model or fix a prompt in one place.

**Keep reliability front and centre.** The framework doesn't excuse you from the production discipline: structured/validated outputs at each boundary, error handling on every external call, max-iterations and cost limits on agents, and observability. Wire these into your LangChain components just as you did by hand. A LangChain pipeline is exactly as reliable as the guards you put in it.

**Trace and debug with LangSmith.** Set up LangChain's tracing so you can see every step's input, output, token cost, and latency. When a chain or agent misbehaves, the trace shows you *where*, indispensable for debugging the abstraction. Observability turns "the agent did something weird" into "step 3 got malformed input from step 2".

Today: take one real task, decide chain-vs-agent (and justify it), build it as a clean composition of small components with reliability guards at each boundary, and enable tracing to inspect its execution. Then deliberately break one step and use the trace to locate the failure. You now wield LangChain with judgment, not just by copying examples.

items.title: Day 7 - LangChain basics
items.body:
## Ship it: a LangChain-powered automation

Wrap Week 11 with a committed automation rebuilt on LangChain, demonstrating that you can use the framework with understanding and judgment.

**What to ship.** A real automation (rebuild an earlier one, or a new piece of your client automation) using LangChain components:
- A **chain or agent** chosen deliberately for the task, with a one-line justification of *why* that pattern.
- **Validated structured output** via an output parser / `with_structured_output`.
- If conversational, **memory** (bounded appropriately); if multi-tool, **tools** via the `@tool` decorator with crisp descriptions.
- **Reliability guards** (validation per boundary, error handling, agent iteration/cost limits) and **tracing** enabled.

**How to ship it.**

```bash
git add langchain-automation/ README.md
git commit -m "Week 11: LangChain automation (chain-vs-agent judgment, structured output, traced)"
git push
```

The README should state the chain-vs-agent decision and why, the components used, and the reliability measures.

**Why this matters.** LangChain is the lingua franca of a huge amount of AI engineering, knowing it makes you employable and lets you build complex systems fast. But your real edge is using it *on top of* first-principles understanding: you know what the abstractions do, when to use a chain vs an agent, and how to debug when they break, which most framework-first learners can't. That judgment is what separates an AI engineer from someone copying LangChain tutorials.

Next week you build your **first fully autonomous agent**, a research agent that takes a topic, searches, reads, synthesises, and writes a report, putting the agent skills to work on a genuinely useful, end-to-end task.

weeks.title: Building your first autonomous agent
weeks.context:
An autonomous agent operates without human intervention from start to finish on multi-step tasks. This week you build one that is genuinely useful: a research agent that takes a topic, searches the web, reads the most relevant pages, synthesises the information, and writes a structured research report.

The architecture: a ReAct loop with 3 tools (web search, page reader, write-report), a system prompt that defines the research process and output format, and a stopping condition when the model decides it has enough information. The challenge is reliability, agents fail in unpredictable ways, and you need to build monitoring and guardrails from the start.

You also learn the concept of agent evaluation: how do you measure whether an agent is doing a good job? You build a small test harness that runs the agent on 5 known tasks and scores the output quality.

days.title: Design your agent

items.title: Design your agent
items.body:
## Design your agent before you build it

This week you build a genuinely useful autonomous agent: a **research agent** that takes a topic, searches the web, reads the best sources, synthesises what it found, and writes a structured report, all without you in the loop. But the first day isn't code. It's **design**, because the difference between an agent that works and one that loops uselessly is almost always the design, not the implementation.

**Define the task crisply.** What exactly does the agent take in, and produce out? "Given a topic, produce a 1-page structured research report with an overview, 3–5 key findings (each with a source), and a short summary." A sharp input/output contract is the spec everything else serves. Vague goals ("research stuff") produce vague, unreliable agents.

**Decide the tools.** An agent is its tools. For research, three are enough: **web_search** (find relevant pages), **read_page** (fetch and clean a page's content), and **write_report** (produce the structured output). Resist tool sprawl, more tools means more ways to choose wrong and more cost. The minimal toolset that can accomplish the task is the right one.

**Write the system prompt as the agent's job description.** The system prompt defines the agent's role, its process, and its limits: "You are a research assistant. Given a topic: search for sources, read the most relevant, then write a structured report citing your sources. Use only information you actually read. Stop when you have enough for a solid report." This is where you encode the *strategy* and the guardrails (cite sources, don't fabricate, know when to stop).

**Plan the loop and its bounds up front.** Sketch the expected flow (search → read 2–3 pages → maybe search again → write) and set bounds *before* coding: max iterations, max pages read, a cost ceiling. Knowing the shape of a good run lets you recognise a bad one. Design the success path *and* the failure stops together.

Today: write your agent's design doc, the input/output contract, the tool list (name + purpose each), the system prompt, and the planned loop with its limits. Commit it. A good design doc makes the rest of the week implementation; a missing one makes it debugging chaos.

days.title: Implement the tools

items.title: Implement the tools
items.body:
## Implement the tools: the agent's hands

An agent can only do what its tools let it do, so today you build the tools *well and independently*, before wiring them into the loop. The discipline: each tool must work reliably on its own, because an agent built on flaky tools is flaky no matter how good its reasoning.

**Build and test each tool in isolation.** For the research agent: **web_search(query)** returns a list of relevant results (title, URL, snippet), via a search API. **read_page(url)** fetches the page (httpx/Playwright), reduces it to clean text (Week 7), and returns it, handling the page that 404s, blocks, or is empty. **write_report(findings)** takes structured findings and produces the final report. Build each as a plain function and test it directly with real inputs *before* the agent ever calls it. A tool you haven't tested standalone is a bug you'll misdiagnose as an agent problem.

**Return clean, model-friendly output.** Tools feed their results back into the model's context, so what they return matters. Keep it concise and structured: search returns a short list, not a wall of HTML; read_page returns clean text trimmed to a sensible length (a 50-page document dumped into context wastes tokens and may exceed limits). Tool output is part of the prompt, treat it with the same economy.

**Handle failure inside the tool, return errors as data.** Each tool will fail sometimes (no results, page unreachable, timeout). Don't let it crash, *catch* the failure and return a clear message the model can read: "No results found" / "Page could not be loaded." A tool that returns its error lets the agent adapt (try another query, another source); a tool that throws kills the run. This is what makes the agent resilient.

**Mind cost and limits per tool.** read_page on a giant page is expensive in tokens; cap the length it returns. search that returns 50 results bloats context; return the top 5. Building these limits into the tools keeps the whole agent affordable, the per-tool economy compounds across an agent's many iterations.

Today: implement and individually test each of your agent's tools with real inputs, including failure cases (a dead URL, a no-result query). Confirm each returns clean, bounded, model-friendly output and never crashes. Solid tools are 80% of a solid agent.

items.body:
[CODE] Create research_tools.py:

import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
from langchain_core.tools import tool

@tool
def search_web(query: str) -> str:
 '''Search the web using DuckDuckGo and return top result URLs.'''
 url = f'https://html.duckduckgo.com/html/?q={query.replace(" ", "+")}'
 r = requests.get(url, headers={'User-Agent': 'Mozilla/5.0'})
 soup = BeautifulSoup(r.text, 'html.parser')
 links = soup.select('.result__url')[:3]
 return '\n'.join(l.text.strip() for l in links)

@tool
def read_url(url: str) -> str:
 '''Read the text content of a webpage. Returns first 2000 characters.'''
 try:
 r = requests.get(url, timeout=10, headers={'User-Agent': 'Mozilla/5.0'})
 soup = BeautifulSoup(r.text, 'html.parser')
 return soup.get_text()[:2000]
 except Exception as e:
 return f'Could not read page: {e}'

@tool
def save_file(filename: str, content: str) -> str:
 '''Save content to a file in the current directory.'''
 with open(filename, 'w') as f:
 f.write(content)
 return f'File saved: {filename}'

items.title: Wire up the agent
items.body:
## Wire up the agent: tools plus loop equals autonomy

With tested tools and a design doc, today you assemble the agent, the loop that lets the model use your tools autonomously until the task is done. You can use LangChain's agent executor (Week 11) or your hand-built loop (Week 6); either way, the wiring is where design becomes a working system.

**Connect tools, model, and system prompt.** Register your tools (name, description, schema, Week 6/11), set your system prompt (the job description from Day 1), and start the loop: send the task + tools + history → model reasons and requests a tool → your code runs it → result goes back → repeat until the model produces the final report. The design doc told you what *should* happen; now you watch what *does*.

**Watch it run, read the trace.** The first runs are about observation, not perfection. Enable tracing/logging and read the agent's actual behaviour: Does it search sensibly? Read relevant pages? Stop at the right time, or thrash? Reading the Thought→Action→Observation trace shows you exactly where its reasoning is good and where it's off. This is the most instructive part of agent-building, you're debugging *reasoning*, not just code.

**Expect, and diagnose, imperfection.** First-run agents misbehave in characteristic ways: searching with poor queries, reading irrelevant pages, looping without progress, or finishing too early with thin findings. Each points to a fix, usually in the *system prompt* or *tool descriptions*, not the loop mechanics. "It reads junk pages" → improve read_page's relevance or the prompt's instruction to pick the best source. Tuning the prompt against observed behaviour is the core skill.

**Get the structured output right.** The agent's final answer should be your defined report structure (validated), not free prose, so downstream code (or a human) can use it reliably. Wire the write_report tool / output parser so the run *ends* in a clean structured report. An agent that does great research but returns an unstructured ramble isn't done.

Today: wire up the full agent and run it on one topic end-to-end, producing a structured report. Read the trace and write down its three biggest behavioural flaws. Don't fix everything yet, just get it running and *understand* how it behaves. Tomorrow you make it robust.

days.title: Add error handling and limits
days.summary: Agents can loop forever or crash. Guard against both.

items.title: Add error handling and limits
items.body:
## Error handling and limits: making the agent safe to run

A working agent and a *deployable* agent are different things. Autonomous agents can loop forever, rack up cost, take bad actions, and fail in ways single calls never do. Today you add the bounds and error handling that turn a clever demo into something you can run unattended without fear.

**Hard limits, non-negotiable.** Every autonomous agent needs: a **max-iteration cap** (after N loops, stop and return the best result so far, never loop infinitely), a **cost/token budget** (track spend per run; abort if it exceeds a ceiling), and a **max-resources** bound (e.g. read at most 5 pages). These prevent the two classic agent disasters, the infinite loop and the runaway bill. Set them generously enough to finish real tasks, tight enough to catch runaway behaviour.

**Graceful degradation, not crashing.** When a tool fails, the agent should adapt, not die. Return tool errors to the model as data (Day 2) so it can try another approach. And when the agent *can't* complete the task (no good sources found, hit the iteration cap), it should return a clear, honest partial result ("here's what I found; I couldn't verify X") rather than crashing or fabricating. An agent that fails gracefully and honestly is far more useful than one that either crashes or confidently invents.

**Guard consequential actions.** A research agent is low-stakes (it reads and writes), but the principle generalises: any tool with real-world effects (sending, paying, deleting, writing to production) needs validation and often confirmation before the agent fires it. Never give an under-supervised agent an unbounded destructive tool. Scope tools to the minimum power needed.

**Anti-hallucination for research specifically.** The research agent's integrity risk is fabricating findings or sources. Enforce: cite the source URL for every finding, instruct "use only what you actually read", and (optionally) verify each cited claim appears in the read content. A research report with fake citations is worse than no report, the guardrail here is the product's credibility.

Today: add the full safety layer, iteration cap, cost budget, page limit, graceful tool-failure handling, honest partial-result behaviour, and source-citation enforcement. Then deliberately make a tool fail (break the search) and confirm the agent degrades gracefully and reports honestly instead of crashing or fabricating.

days.title: Test on 3 different topics
days.summary: Run your agent 3 times. Observe where it succeeds and where it fails.

items.title: Test on 3 different topics
items.body:
## Test on real, varied topics: where agents really get judged

A single successful run proves nothing about an agent, autonomous systems are defined by their behaviour across *varied* inputs, including the hard ones. Today you test your research agent on several different topics and use what breaks to harden it. This is how agent reliability is actually earned.

**Choose deliberately diverse topics.** Pick at least three that stress different things: a **well-documented** topic (lots of good sources, the happy path), an **obscure or niche** topic (few sources, where it must cope with thin information), and an **ambiguous** topic (a term with multiple meanings, where search returns mixed results). Each exposes different weaknesses, breadth of testing is what reveals an agent's true reliability, not depth on one easy case.

**Evaluate each run honestly.** For every topic, judge: Are the findings *accurate* and actually supported by the cited sources (check a couple)? Is the report *complete* and well-structured? Did the agent *behave well* (sensible searches, relevant reads, stopped appropriately, stayed within limits)? What did it *cost* and how long did it take? Honest evaluation, including checking citations against sources, is the only way to know if the agent is trustworthy or just plausible-looking.

**Turn failures into fixes.** Each weakness maps to an improvement, usually in the prompt or tools, rarely the loop. Reads irrelevant pages → sharpen source-selection in the prompt or read_page. Fabricates on thin topics → strengthen the "only what you read" instruction and the honest-partial behaviour. Poor queries → give query-formulation guidance. Iterate: fix, re-test on all topics, confirm you didn't regress the ones that worked. This test-fix-retest loop is the actual work of building a reliable agent.

**Know your agent's envelope.** After testing, you should be able to state plainly: what kinds of topics it handles well, where it struggles, its typical cost and time, and what a user should *not* rely on it for. This honest "envelope" is what makes the agent professionally usable, and it's exactly what you'd tell a client. An agent whose limits you know is trustworthy; one you've only run once is not.

Today: run your agent on 3+ deliberately varied topics, evaluate each honestly (including checking citations), fix the weaknesses you find, and re-test. Write down the agent's reliability envelope, where it's strong, where it's weak, its cost and time. That measured honesty is the mark of an engineer.

items.title: Day 6 - Building your first autonomous agent
items.body:
## Consolidate: a polished, dependable research agent

Today you bring the week together into a polished agent you'd be proud to demo or ship, and reflect on what you've learned about building autonomous systems, because the meta-lessons here transfer to every agent you'll build.

**Polish to dependable.** Take everything, tested tools, tuned prompt, safety limits, graceful failure, citation enforcement, and make the agent dependable across its envelope. The final run should reliably produce accurate, well-structured, source-cited reports on topics within its scope, stay within cost and iteration bounds, and fail honestly outside its scope. Dependable-within-a-known-envelope is the realistic, professional bar, not "works on everything", which no agent achieves.

**Improve the output quality.** A research agent's value is in its *report*. Polish the structure (clear overview, well-organised findings, each with a citation, a crisp summary), and make it genuinely useful, the kind of brief that saves someone an hour. The synthesis quality (does it actually integrate sources into insight, not just list them?) is where a good research agent earns its keep. Tune the write_report step and prompt for this.

**Reflect on the agent-building lessons.** You've now lived the core truths: design and prompt matter more than loop mechanics; tools must be reliable independently; bounds and graceful failure are mandatory; reasoning is debugged by reading traces; and reliability is proven across varied tests, not one demo. Write these down, they're the durable skills, transferable to *any* agent (a coding agent, a support agent, a data agent), long after this specific research agent fades.

**Mind cost-effectiveness.** Step back: is the agent *worth* its cost and latency for the value it delivers? Sometimes a simpler chain or a cheaper model does nearly as well for a fraction of the cost. Knowing when an agent is the right tool, and when it's overkill, is senior judgment. Note where your agent could be simpler or cheaper without losing much.

Today: polish your agent into a dependable, well-documented tool with genuinely useful report output, and write a short reflection on the agent-building principles you've internalised. You've gone from "I can call an AI" to "I can design, build, bound, and validate an autonomous system", a real engineering capability.

items.title: Day 7 - Building your first autonomous agent
items.body:
## Ship it: a working autonomous research agent

Wrap Week 12 with a committed, dependable autonomous agent, a portfolio-grade piece that proves you can build, not just describe, agentic systems.

**What to ship.**
- The **research agent**: takes a topic, searches, reads sources, synthesises, and produces a **structured, source-cited report**, autonomously.
- **Tools** (search, read, write_report) each tested independently and returning clean, bounded, error-as-data output.
- A **safety layer**: max-iteration cap, cost budget, resource limits, graceful tool-failure handling, honest partial results, and enforced source citations (anti-fabrication).
- A documented **reliability envelope**: tested on 3+ varied topics, with notes on where it's strong/weak and its typical cost and time.

**How to ship it.**

```bash
git add research-agent/ README.md
git commit -m "Week 12: autonomous research agent (search-read-synthesise, bounded, cited, tested)"
git push
```

The README should include the design (task, tools, system prompt), the safety bounds, sample output, and the honest reliability envelope.

**Why this matters.** A working, bounded, *validated* autonomous agent is one of the most impressive things in an AI portfolio, most people can demo a chatbot; few can build an agent that does real multi-step work reliably and *knows its own limits*. You designed it, built reliable tools, bounded it, and proved its behaviour across varied tests. That's genuine AI engineering.

Next week you move from a single agent to **orchestrating multi-step workflows**, with LangGraph: branching, parallel steps, retries, and fallbacks, the patterns that let you build complex, resilient pipelines out of the agent and chain skills you now have.

weeks.title: Multi-step workflows and orchestration
weeks.context:
Multi-step workflows chain multiple AI calls, external API calls, database operations, and conditional logic together into a coherent pipeline. As automations grow more complex, you need orchestration, a way to manage state, handle failures at any step, and retry or route around errors without starting from scratch.

Orchestration patterns: sequential (A → B → C), parallel (A and B run simultaneously, then C waits for both), conditional (if A returns X, go to B, else go to C), and fan-out/fan-in (process N items in parallel, aggregate results). The right pattern depends on the task, sequential is simplest, parallel is fastest when steps are independent.

This week you build a multi-step content production workflow using Prefect (a Python orchestration framework) and compare it to building the same workflow manually. You also learn state management: how to track which steps have completed when a workflow is interrupted and needs to resume.

days.title: Workflow graphs with LangGraph

items.title: Workflow graphs with LangGraph
items.body:
## Orchestration and workflow graphs with LangGraph

As automations grow, "a chain of steps" becomes too simple, you need **orchestration**: managing state across many steps, branching on conditions, running steps in parallel, and recovering from failures without restarting. **LangGraph** models a workflow as a **graph** of nodes and edges, which is exactly the right abstraction for complex, stateful, resilient pipelines.

**Why a graph, not a line.** A simple chain is a straight line (A→B→C). Real workflows branch ("if it's an invoice, do X; if a contract, do Y"), loop (retry, or an agent's iterate-until-done), run things in parallel, and need to track shared **state** as data flows through. A graph, **nodes** (steps) connected by **edges** (transitions, including conditional ones) that share a state object, captures all of this naturally. LangGraph is purpose-built for it, and it's what underlies robust agent and pipeline systems.

**The core concepts.** A LangGraph workflow has: a **state** (a shared object, e.g. a dict/typed schema, that every node reads and updates), **nodes** (functions that take the state, do work, and return updates), and **edges** (which node runs next, possibly **conditional** on the state). You define the graph, then invoke it with an initial state; it runs the nodes along the edges until it reaches an end. This explicit state + graph structure is what makes complex workflows debuggable and resilient.

**State is the heart of it.** Unlike a stateless chain, a graph threads a **shared state** through every step, accumulating results, tracking status, holding everything the workflow needs. Designing this state schema well (what does each step need to read and write?) is the key design task, get it right and the nodes become simple. It's the same "memory" idea from Week 11, now structured as the workflow's backbone.

**Why this matters for production.** Graph orchestration gives you what production needs: explicit state you can inspect and persist (resume after a crash), clear branching logic, the ability to retry or route around a failed node without restarting the whole pipeline, and traceability. It's the framework that turns the patterns you've built into resilient, complex systems.

Today: build a minimal LangGraph workflow, define a small state schema, two or three nodes that read and update it, and edges connecting them, then run it and inspect the final state. Seeing data flow through a graph, accumulating in shared state, is the foundation for everything this week.

[CODE] Run: pip install langgraph

Create graph_workflow.py:

from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, END
from typing import TypedDict

class State(TypedDict):
 text: str
 summary: str
 label: str

def summarise(state: State) -> State:
 # Call GPT to summarise state['text']
 state['summary'] = 'This is a summary.'
 return state

def classify(state: State) -> State:
 state['label'] = 'URGENT'
 return state

workflow = StateGraph(State)
workflow.add_node('summarise', summarise)
workflow.add_node('classify', classify)
workflow.set_entry_point('summarise')
workflow.add_edge('summarise', 'classify')
workflow.add_edge('classify', END)

app = workflow.compile()
result = app.invoke({'text': 'Server is down', 'summary': '', 'label': ''})
print(result)

days.title: Conditional branching
days.summary: Route the workflow differently based on intermediate results.

items.title: Conditional branching
items.body:
## Conditional branching: workflows that make decisions

Linear workflows do the same steps every time; real ones **branch**, taking different paths based on the data. Conditional branching is how a workflow handles variety (different document types, different priorities, different outcomes) explicitly and reliably, encoding your *known* decision logic rather than leaving it to an agent's improvisation.

**Conditional edges.** In LangGraph, a **conditional edge** routes to different next-nodes based on the current state: a routing function reads the state and returns which node to go to next. "After classifying the document, if it's an invoice → invoice_node; if a contract → contract_node; else → review_node." The branch is explicit code reading explicit state, predictable and debuggable, unlike an agent deciding on the fly.

**Branch on AI output, safely.** A powerful pattern: an AI node classifies or decides, writes its result to state, and a conditional edge routes on it. This combines AI judgment (the classification) with deterministic control flow (the routing), the clean reasoner/executor split again, now at the workflow level. The key reliability point: route on *validated* AI output (a value from your fixed enum), and always have a default/fallback branch for the unexpected, so an out-of-range classification goes somewhere safe rather than crashing the graph.

**Branches for success vs failure.** Branching isn't only about data type, it's how you handle outcomes. After a node runs, branch on whether it succeeded: success → continue; failure → a recovery or escalation path; low-confidence → a human-review node. Modelling failure paths as explicit branches (rather than buried try/excepts) makes a workflow's resilience visible and designed, not accidental.

**Keep the logic readable.** As branches multiply, a workflow can become a tangle. Keep routing functions small and named, document each branch's condition, and prefer a few clear decision points over deeply nested conditions. A workflow graph you can read at a glance is one you can maintain; a spaghetti graph is a liability. (LangGraph's visualisation helps, you can render the graph to see its structure.)

Today: extend your workflow with a conditional branch, an AI (or rule) node writes a decision to state, and a conditional edge routes to different nodes based on it, with a default branch for the unexpected. Test it with inputs that take each path, including one that hits the default. You've built a workflow that *decides*.

days.title: Parallel steps
days.summary: Run two steps at the same time to cut pipeline duration.

items.title: Parallel steps
items.body:
## Parallel steps: doing independent work at once

When a workflow has steps that don't depend on each other, running them **in parallel** instead of one-after-another can dramatically cut total time, important when each step is a slow AI or API call. Recognising and exploiting parallelism is a key skill for building responsive, efficient pipelines.

**Spot the independence.** Steps can run in parallel only if neither needs the other's output. "Summarise the document" and "extract its metadata" are independent, do them at once. "Extract data" then "validate that data" are *not*, the second needs the first. The analysis is: draw the dependency graph; anything not on the same dependency chain can run concurrently. This is the same thinking as parallelising any work.

**Parallel patterns in orchestration.** A common shape is **fan-out / fan-in**: split into several parallel branches (fan-out), each doing independent work, then **combine** their results in a downstream node (fan-in). For example: given a document, simultaneously summarise it, extract entities, and classify it; then a final node assembles all three into one record. LangGraph supports parallel node execution and gathering the results back into shared state. The time saving is roughly the difference between the *sum* of the steps and the *longest* single step.

**The payoff and the cost.** Parallelism cuts **latency** (a 3-step sequence of 5-second calls takes 15s serial, ~5s parallel), which matters for user-facing or high-volume automations. But it doesn't cut *total work or cost*, you still make all the calls, and you may hit **rate limits** faster by firing many at once. Balance concurrency against API limits (cap how many run simultaneously), and remember parallelism helps *time*, not *money*.

**Manage shared state carefully.** When parallel branches write to shared state, avoid them clobbering each other, have each write to its own key, and combine in the fan-in node. Race conditions in workflow state are a subtle bug class; clean separation of what each branch owns prevents them (the same discipline as concurrent writes to a spreadsheet/database from Week 10).

Today: identify independent steps in one of your workflows and restructure them to run in parallel (fan-out), then fan-in to combine results. Measure the latency before and after. Seeing a multi-step workflow finish in the time of its slowest step, instead of the sum, is the lesson, and a real tool for responsive automations.

[CODE] Create parallel_pipeline.py:

import asyncio
from openai import AsyncOpenAI
from dotenv import load_dotenv
import os

load_dotenv()
client = AsyncOpenAI(api_key=os.getenv('OPENAI_API_KEY'))

async def summarise(text):
 r = await client.chat.completions.create(
 model='gpt-4o-mini',
 messages=[{'role':'system','content':'Summarise in one sentence.'},{'role':'user','content':text}]
 )
 return r.choices[0].message.content

async def classify(text):
 r = await client.chat.completions.create(
 model='gpt-4o-mini',
 messages=[{'role':'system','content':'Reply URGENT, NORMAL, or LOW only.'},{'role':'user','content':text}]
 )
 return r.choices[0].message.content

async def process(text):
 summary, label = await asyncio.gather(summarise(text), classify(text))
 return {'summary': summary, 'label': label}

result = asyncio.run(process('Our database crashed and all users are offline.'))
print(result) # Both calls ran simultaneously

days.title: Retry and fallback logic
days.summary: What happens when a step fails? The pipeline must recover.

items.title: Retry and fallback logic
items.body:
## Retry and fallback: resilience when steps fail

In production, steps *will* fail, an API times out, the model returns junk, a rate limit hits, a service is briefly down. **Retry and fallback** logic is what lets a workflow recover from these transient and partial failures instead of collapsing. This is the difference between an automation that needs babysitting and one that runs itself for months.

**Retry with backoff, for transient failures.** Many failures are temporary, a timeout, a 429 rate limit, a brief 5xx. The right response is to **retry**, but smartly: wait before retrying (**exponential backoff**: 1s, then 2s, then 4s) so you don't hammer a struggling service, cap the number of attempts, and only retry failures that are actually transient (don't retry a 400 bad-request, it'll fail identically). Built into each external-call node, retry-with-backoff silently absorbs the everyday flakiness of networks and APIs.

**Fallbacks, when the primary path can't deliver.** When retries are exhausted or a whole approach fails, a **fallback** provides an alternative: a cheaper/different model if the primary is down, a simpler method if the sophisticated one fails, a cached or default result if fresh data is unavailable, or routing to a human. Fallbacks turn "the workflow failed" into "the workflow degraded gracefully." Designing the fallback for each critical step is what keeps the pipeline producing *something* useful under adverse conditions.

**Decide failure policy per step.** Not every step deserves the same treatment. For each, decide: retry (how many times, what backoff)? fall back (to what)? or fail the workflow (when the step is essential and has no alternative)? And crucially, **fail loud**, when a step ultimately can't be handled, the workflow should record it and alert, not swallow it silently. Modelling these policies explicitly (often as conditional edges to retry/fallback/escalate nodes) makes resilience a designed property, not luck.

**Idempotency makes retries safe.** Retrying a step that has side effects (sent an email, wrote a row) can cause duplicates. Design steps so re-running is safe, check-before-act, use idempotency keys, so retry and fallback logic can't cause the very damage it's meant to prevent. This is the Week 2/10 idempotency lesson, now essential because orchestration *will* re-run things.

Today: add retry-with-backoff to your workflow's external-call nodes and a fallback path for one critical step (e.g. a cheaper model or a default result), plus loud alerting when a step ultimately fails. Simulate failures (force a timeout, force junk output) and confirm the workflow recovers or degrades gracefully rather than crashing.

items.title: Build a multi-stage content pipeline
items.body:
## Build: a multi-stage content pipeline

Today you assemble the week's orchestration skills into a real, multi-stage pipeline, a content pipeline that takes an input (a topic, a transcript, raw notes) and produces polished, multi-format output through several coordinated stages. It's a genuinely sellable automation and a showcase of branching, parallelism, retries, and state.

**A concrete pipeline.** For example: given a topic or source material → **research/gather** (or ingest) → **draft** the core content → **fan-out in parallel** to derive formats (a blog post, a summary, social posts, an email) → **quality-check** each (an AI review node, with a branch to revise if it fails) → **assemble and format** the final outputs. Each stage is a node; the whole thing is a LangGraph workflow with shared state carrying the content as it's transformed. This is the kind of pipeline content teams pay real money to automate.

**Use every orchestration tool deliberately.** *State* carries the content and metadata through all stages. *Conditional branching* routes on quality checks (pass → continue, fail → revise) and content type. *Parallel steps* generate the multiple formats at once (they're independent). *Retry/fallback* handle the inevitable API hiccups across the many AI calls. Building this pipeline forces you to apply each pattern in concert, which is exactly how production systems use them, together, not in isolation.

**Design the state schema first.** As in Day 1, the state is the backbone: what does the pipeline need to hold? The source material, the draft, each derived format, quality-check results, status flags. Designing this schema before the nodes makes each node simple (read these keys, write those). A muddled state schema makes the whole pipeline hard to reason about, so spend the design time here.

**Quality gates with revise loops.** A powerful pattern: after generating content, an AI **quality-check** node scores it; a conditional edge sends failures back to a **revise** node (with the critique) and passes successes forward, capped so it can't loop forever. This self-correcting loop materially improves output quality and is a great demonstration of conditional + iterative orchestration. It's the reflection pattern from agents, applied as explicit workflow structure.

Today: build the multi-stage content pipeline end-to-end in LangGraph, with a designed state schema, parallel format generation, a quality-check-and-revise branch, and retry/fallback on AI calls. Run real input through it and inspect the state at each stage. You've built a production-shaped orchestrated pipeline, not just a chain.

items.title: Day 6 - Multi-step workflows and orchestration
items.body:
## Consolidate: design resilient, observable workflows

Today you step back from individual patterns to the *craft* of orchestration, designing workflows that are resilient, observable, and maintainable, because as systems grow, these qualities decide whether they're an asset or a liability.

**Design state and structure first.** The recurring lesson: a workflow's quality is mostly decided before you write the nodes, in the **state schema** and the **graph structure**. A clean, well-named state and a clear graph (readable branches, identified parallelism, explicit failure paths) make nodes simple and the whole thing maintainable. Practise sketching the state and graph for a workflow *before* coding it; that design discipline is what keeps complex orchestration from becoming a tangle.

**Make resilience a designed property.** Pull together the week's resilience patterns into a checklist you apply to every workflow: external calls have retry+backoff; critical steps have fallbacks; failures route to explicit recovery/escalation nodes (and fail loud); steps are idempotent so retries are safe; and there are hard bounds on any loops. A workflow where these are *designed in* (visible as nodes and edges) is resilient by construction; one where they're afterthoughts is fragile.

**Observability is not optional.** A complex workflow you can't see into is impossible to debug or trust in production. Build in: structured **logging** at each node (what it received, did, produced), **tracing** (LangSmith or similar) to see the full execution path and timings, and a **run summary** (which path it took, what it cost, what failed). When something goes wrong at 3 a.m., observability is the difference between a five-minute fix and an outage. This previews Week 17, here you wire it into the orchestration itself.

**Manage cost and latency consciously.** Multi-step, multi-call workflows can get expensive and slow. Review each: can a step use a cheaper model? Can independent steps run in parallel? Can you cache or skip redundant work? Is an agent step really needed, or would a fixed chain do? Conscious cost/latency design is what makes an orchestrated system economical at scale, and it's part of pricing client work.

Today: take one of your workflows and do a design review against the resilience checklist and observability requirements, then improve it: tighten the state schema, make failure paths explicit, add per-node logging and a run summary, and find one cost/latency optimisation. You're now designing orchestration like an engineer, for resilience and operability, not just function.

items.title: Day 7 - Multi-step workflows and orchestration
items.body:
## Ship it: an orchestrated multi-step pipeline

Wrap Week 13 with a committed, resilient orchestrated workflow, most likely your multi-stage content pipeline, demonstrating you can build complex, production-shaped systems.

**What to ship.**
- A **LangGraph workflow** with a designed **state schema**, multiple coordinated stages, **conditional branching** (e.g. a quality-check-and-revise loop), and **parallel** steps where work is independent.
- A **resilience layer**: retry-with-backoff on external calls, a fallback for at least one critical step, explicit failure/escalation paths, idempotent steps, and bounded loops.
- **Observability**: per-node logging, tracing, and a run summary (path taken, cost, failures).

**How to ship it.**

```bash
git add orchestration/ README.md
git commit -m "Week 13: orchestrated multi-step pipeline (LangGraph - branching, parallel, retry/fallback, observable)"
git push
```

The README should include the workflow's purpose, a sketch of its graph/state, and its resilience and observability measures.

**Why this matters.** Real-world automations are rarely a single call or a simple chain, they're orchestrated, stateful, branching, resilient pipelines. Being able to *design and build* these (not just wire a quick chain) is what lets you take on substantial, valuable automation projects. Orchestration with explicit state, branching, parallelism, and designed-in resilience is exactly the capability that separates someone who builds toys from someone who builds systems.

Next week you add one of the most important capabilities in modern AI automation: **RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation)**, giving your systems access to large, private knowledge bases so they can answer from *your* documents, accurately and at scale.

weeks.title: RAG, retrieval augmented generation
weeks.context:
RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) is how you give an LLM access to a large knowledge base without putting all of it in the context window. Instead of feeding the model an entire documentation library, you embed the documents into vector representations, store them in a vector database, and at query time retrieve only the most relevant chunks, then send those chunks plus the user's question to the model.

RAG is the dominant pattern for enterprise AI applications: chatbots that answer questions from company documentation, support agents that reference product manuals, search systems that understand natural language. Understanding the full pipeline, chunking, embedding, storing, retrieving, reranking, prompting, lets you build and debug these systems from first principles.

The hardest part of RAG is not the retrieval, it is getting the chunking and retrieval quality right. A RAG system that retrieves the wrong chunks gives the model bad context, which produces confident-sounding but wrong answers. Chunk quality and retrieval quality are the primary levers for RAG accuracy.

days.title: What is RAG and why does it matter

items.title: What is RAG and why does it matter
items.body:
## RAG: giving AI access to your knowledge

A language model only knows what it was trained on, not your company's documents, your client's contracts, or anything private or recent. **RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation)** is the technique that fixes this: it gives the model access to a large, private knowledge base *without* stuffing everything into the prompt. It's one of the most important and commercially valuable patterns in AI automation, the backbone of every "chat with your documents" product.

**The problem RAG solves.** You can't paste a 500-page documentation library, or 10,000 support tickets, into a prompt, it won't fit in the context window, and even if it did, it'd be slow and expensive. But the model needs that knowledge to answer accurately. RAG's insight: don't send *everything*, send only the *relevant* pieces, retrieved on demand for each question.

**The core flow: retrieve, then generate.** RAG has two phases. **Indexing (once):** split your documents into chunks, convert each chunk into a numerical **embedding** that captures its meaning, and store them in a **vector database**. **Querying (per question):** embed the user's question, find the chunks whose embeddings are most similar (the relevant ones), and send *those chunks plus the question* to the model, which answers grounded in them. Retrieve the relevant context, then generate the answer from it, that's RAG.

**Why it's everywhere.** RAG powers customer-support bots that answer from a company's help docs, internal assistants that know company policies, research tools over private papers, "chat with your PDF" apps, any system that must answer accurately from a specific, large, or private body of knowledge. It's accurate (grounded in real documents), scalable (works over millions of chunks), and updatable (add a document, it's instantly available), without retraining the model.

**RAG vs the alternatives.** For knowledge that fits in context, just include it (Week 4's in-context Q&A), simpler, no RAG needed. For a *large or private* knowledge base, RAG is the answer. (Fine-tuning teaches a model a *skill or style*, not facts, and is the wrong tool for "know my documents".) Knowing when RAG is and isn't the right tool is part of the skill.

Today: write up the RAG concept in your own words, the indexing phase and the query phase, and identify one real use case you could build (a bot over your own notes, a client's docs, a product manual). Drawing the retrieve-then-generate flow yourself cements the pattern before you build it.

days.title: Embeddings, turning text into numbers
days.summary: Embeddings are how AI searches for meaning, not keywords.

items.title: Embeddings, turning text into numbers
items.body:
## Embeddings: turning meaning into numbers

RAG's magic rests on **embeddings**, a way to convert text into a list of numbers (a vector) that captures its *meaning*, so that similar meanings produce similar vectors. Understanding embeddings is understanding how retrieval actually finds "relevant" chunks, and it's a concept that powers far more than RAG.

**What an embedding is.** An embedding model takes a piece of text and outputs a fixed-length vector (e.g. 1,536 numbers). The key property: texts with *similar meaning* get vectors that are *close together* in that high-dimensional space, even if they share no words. "How do I reset my password?" and "I forgot my login credentials" land near each other; "what's the weather?" lands far away. The model has learned to place meaning in space, that's what makes semantic search possible.

**Semantic similarity, not keyword matching.** This is the leap beyond traditional search. Keyword search finds documents containing the *words* you typed; embedding (semantic) search finds documents that *mean* the same thing, regardless of wording. That's why RAG can answer a question phrased completely differently from the source document, it matches on meaning. Similarity is measured by the distance/angle between vectors (cosine similarity is the usual metric): closer vectors = more similar meaning.

**How it powers retrieval.** In RAG: at indexing time you embed every document chunk; at query time you embed the question. Retrieval is then "find the chunk vectors closest to the question vector", a fast nearest-neighbour search in vector space. The closest chunks are, by construction, the most semantically relevant, exactly what you want to feed the model. Embeddings turn "find relevant text" into "find nearby vectors", a problem computers solve fast.

**Practicalities.** You get embeddings from an embedding API (providers offer dedicated embedding models, distinct from chat models) or a local model. Each embedding call has a (small) cost, and consistency matters: use the *same* embedding model for your documents and your queries, or the vectors won't be comparable. Chunk size also matters (next lesson): too big and an embedding blurs multiple topics; too small and it loses context.

Today: generate embeddings for a handful of sentences (some similar in meaning, some different), and compute the similarity between pairs. Confirm that meaning-similar sentences score high and unrelated ones score low, even when the words differ. Seeing semantic similarity work numerically is the "aha" behind all of RAG.

items.title: Generate and compare embeddings
items.body:
[CODE] Create embeddings.py:

from openai import OpenAI
from dotenv import load_dotenv
import os
import numpy as np

load_dotenv()
client = OpenAI(api_key=os.getenv('OPENAI_API_KEY'))

def embed(text):
 r = client.embeddings.create(model='text-embedding-3-small', input=text)
 return np.array(r.data[0].embedding)

def similarity(a, b):
 return np.dot(a, b) / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))

e1 = embed('The cat sat on the mat')
e2 = embed('A feline rested on a rug')
e3 = embed('The stock market crashed today')

print('Similar sentences:', similarity(e1, e2)) # ~0.9
print('Different topics:', similarity(e1, e3)) # ~0.2

Nearly identical meaning = high similarity. Different topics = low similarity.

items.title: Build a vector store with FAISS
items.body:
## Building a vector store: indexing your documents

A **vector store** (vector database) holds your document embeddings and makes "find the most similar chunks to this query" fast, even over millions of entries. Today you build one and index real documents, the indexing half of RAG that everything else depends on.

**Chunking: split before you embed.** You don't embed whole documents, you split them into **chunks** (passages of a few hundred words). Why: an embedding captures one coherent meaning, so a chunk should be one topic-sized piece; and retrieval returns chunks, so chunk size controls how focused the retrieved context is. The craft: split on natural boundaries (paragraphs, sections), keep chunks a sensible size, and **overlap** them slightly (so a sentence split across a boundary isn't lost). Bad chunking is the #1 cause of bad RAG, too big blurs topics, too small loses context, so this step matters more than it seems.

**The vector store options.** **FAISS** (a local library) and **ChromaDB** are great for learning and small-to-medium projects, no server, runs on your machine. **Pinecone**, **Weaviate**, and **pgvector** (Postgres) are managed/scalable options for production. They all do the same job: store vectors (with their source text and metadata) and answer nearest-neighbour queries fast. Start local (FAISS/Chroma); reach for a managed store when scale or multi-user access demands it.

**The indexing pipeline.** Put it together: load documents → chunk them → embed each chunk → store each vector *along with its source text and metadata* (which document, which section, useful for citations later) in the vector store. Run once up front; re-run incrementally when documents change. LangChain's document loaders, text splitters, and vector-store integrations make this a handful of lines, but understanding each step is what lets you tune retrieval quality.

**Metadata earns its keep.** Store metadata with each chunk (source, title, date, section). It enables **citations** (tell the user *which* document an answer came from, essential for trust) and **filtered retrieval** (only search a certain document set, or recent ones). Skipping metadata is a common mistake that costs you these later.

Today: build a vector store, take a set of documents (your notes, a few PDFs), chunk them sensibly with overlap, embed the chunks, and store them with metadata in FAISS or ChromaDB. Then run a test query and inspect which chunks come back. Tune your chunking if the retrieved chunks aren't well-focused, that tuning is the real skill.
