items.title: Your automation portfolio
items.body:
## Your automation portfolio: proof you can deliver

Before anyone hires you, they need evidence you can actually build what you promise. Your **portfolio** is that proof, and for automation it's especially powerful because the results are so concrete (time saved, work eliminated). A strong portfolio turns "trust me" into "look what I've already done", which is what wins the first clients.

**Lead with outcomes, not tech.** Each portfolio piece should headline the *result*: "Automated invoice processing, cut a 10-hour/week task to near-zero, 99% accuracy." Then, below, the how (the pipeline, the tools), and ideally a demo or screenshots. A prospective client cares first whether you can solve *their* kind of problem; the technical detail reassures them you did it properly. Structure each piece: problem → solution → result → how, with the result up top.

**You already have the pieces, package them.** Across this course you've built real, demonstrable automations: an n8n workflow, a document processor, a web-scraping bot, a research agent, a RAG system, a deployed pipeline. Each is a portfolio entry. Package 3–5 of your strongest as case studies, with the business framing (even if built on sample/your-own data, present them as "here's a working solution to problem X"). Curation beats volume: a few polished, clearly-explained pieces outperform a dump of repos.

**Make it tangible and verifiable.** Automation portfolios shine when prospects can *see* it work: a short screen-recording (Loom) of the automation running, before/after, sample outputs, a live demo, a clean GitHub repo with a strong README. Tangible proof ("here's a 90-second video of it processing 50 invoices") is far more persuasive than description. Clients believe what they can see.

**Host it where clients look.** A simple portfolio site (or a strong GitHub profile + a Notion page) collecting your case studies, with your contact and a clear "here's what I do for businesses". The goal: when you reach out to a prospect or apply to a gig, you have a link that immediately proves competence. This is your single most important sales asset, the thing that makes a cold contact warm.

Today: build your automation portfolio, package 3–5 of your course builds as outcome-led case studies (problem → solution → result → how), with at least one tangible demo (a Loom video or live demo) and clean repos, hosted on a simple site or profile. This is the proof that converts interest into hiring, invest in making it clear and concrete.

items.title: Upwork profile and first proposals
items.body:
## Finding clients and writing proposals that win

With a portfolio in hand, you need clients, and the fastest starting point for most automation builders is freelance platforms (**Upwork**, and similar) plus direct outreach. Today is about getting in front of prospects and writing proposals that actually win the job, a learnable skill with clear patterns.

**Set up a focused profile.** On Upwork (or wherever), your profile should be **specific**, not "I do everything tech" but "I build AI automations that eliminate repetitive business tasks, document processing, data entry, reporting." A clear niche makes you the obvious choice for that problem and easier to remember and refer. Lead with outcomes and link your portfolio. A focused specialist out-earns a vague generalist.

**Where the work is.** Beyond Upwork: direct outreach to small businesses with visible manual-work pain (the opportunity radar, applied to real companies), your existing network (the warmest leads, people who already trust you), and communities where business owners gather. Early on, *volume and warmth* matter, more conversations, especially with people who know you, beat waiting for the perfect inbound lead. Your first client is often someone you already know with a problem you can now solve.

**Proposals: be specific, show you understood.** The winning proposal isn't a generic blurb, it's evidence you *understood this client's specific problem* and can solve it. Reference *their* situation ("you mentioned spending hours manually entering orders, here's how I'd automate exactly that"), outline a concrete approach, point to a relevant portfolio piece, and be clear on next steps. Most proposals are lazy and generic; a specific, problem-focused one stands out immediately. Quality and relevance beat volume.

**Price the value, start with momentum.** Early on, your goal is *proof and momentum*, the first few projects, testimonials, and case studies, sometimes worth pricing low (or a free build in exchange for a case study, the Week 19 option). But quickly move to **value-based** thinking: if you save a business $2,000/month, charging $1,500 to build it is a bargain *for them*, even though it took you days. Don't price your *time*; price the *value delivered*. This shift is what turns freelancing into real income.

Today: set up a focused freelance profile (or refine your outreach pitch) specialised in automation, identify 5 concrete prospects (platform gigs, businesses with visible pain, or warm contacts), and write *one* genuinely specific, problem-focused proposal/pitch for a real opportunity, referencing the prospect's situation and a relevant portfolio piece. Sending one *good* proposal teaches more than reading about ten.

days.title: Discovery calls and scoping projects
days.summary: How to turn an inquiry into a paid project.

items.title: Discovery calls and scoping projects
items.body:
## Discovery and scoping: the skill that prevents disasters

The moment a prospect is interested, two skills determine whether the project succeeds or becomes a nightmare: **discovery** (truly understanding their problem) and **scoping** (defining exactly what you'll deliver). Most failed client projects fail *here*, in vague understanding and unbounded scope, not in the building. Getting this right protects both you and the client.

**Discovery: understand before you propose.** A discovery call is about *listening*, not pitching. Understand: what's the actual task and current process? How often, how much time, what does it cost them? What does a *good* outcome look like to them? What's their data like (where, what format, how messy)? What are the edge cases and exceptions? You can't scope or price what you don't understand, and the messy reality (the weird exceptions, the bad data) is exactly what determines effort. Ask, and listen, before you commit to anything.

**Scope explicitly, in writing.** Define precisely what you *will* deliver, and just as importantly what you *won't*. "I'll automate invoice processing for PDF invoices from your top 10 vendors, extracting these 6 fields into your spreadsheet, with a review queue for low-confidence cases. Not included: scanned/handwritten invoices, integration with your accounting software." A written scope is the contract that prevents the project from sprawling, it's what protects you from endless "can it also...?" and protects the client from misaligned expectations. Vague scope is the #1 cause of unhappy projects.

**Set realistic expectations about AI.** Clients often expect AI to be 100% perfect or fully autonomous. Be honest up front: AI automation is highly reliable but *not* infallible, so good designs include validation and human-in-the-loop for edge cases (everything you learned). Setting this expectation early ("it'll handle ~95% automatically and flag the rest for a quick human check") prevents the disappointment of a client expecting magic. Under-promise on perfection, over-deliver on reliability, honesty here builds trust and repeat work.

**Price and contract clearly.** With scope understood, price it (value-based, anchored to the saving you'll deliver), and put the essentials in writing: deliverables, timeline, price, what's included/excluded, and terms (a deposit, milestones). Even a lightweight written agreement prevents most disputes. Professionalism in scoping and contracting signals you're someone serious to work with, which itself justifies higher rates.

Today: prepare your **discovery and scoping toolkit**, a short list of discovery questions you'll always ask (process, frequency, cost, data, edge cases, success criteria), and a simple **scope template** (deliverables, explicitly-excluded, timeline, price, AI-reliability expectation). If you have a real prospect, run a discovery conversation and draft a scoped proposal. These two skills prevent more project disasters than any technical ability.

days.title: Productise, turn one project into a product
days.summary: The fastest way to scale: sell the same automation to many clients.

items.title: Productise, turn one project into a product
items.body:
## Productising: from custom builds to scalable income

Custom client projects earn money but don't *scale*, your income is capped by your hours. **Productising**, turning a repeatable solution into a product or repeatable offering, is how automation builders break that ceiling. You don't need to do it yet, but understanding the path shapes smarter choices now.

**Spot the repeatable pattern.** After a few client projects, you'll notice the *same problem* recurring across businesses, invoice processing, lead enrichment, report generation. That repetition is the productisation signal: instead of building it bespoke every time, build it *once, well*, and offer it as a near-standard solution you configure per client. The first build is custom; the fifth should be 80% reuse. Recognising and exploiting that reuse is the leverage.

**The productisation ladder.** There's a spectrum from pure services to pure product: **bespoke project** (fully custom, doesn't scale) → **productised service** (a fixed-scope, fixed-price offering you deliver repeatably, "invoice automation setup, $X, configured for your vendors") → **template/toolkit** (a reusable solution you adapt quickly) → **SaaS product** (clients self-serve a tool you built once, scales without your time). Each step up trades customisation for scalability. Most successful solo automation builders live in the *productised service* zone, the sweet spot of repeatability and good margins, without the burden of building and supporting a full SaaS.

**Productised services: the practical win.** The most accessible leverage is the productised service, a clearly-defined offering with a fixed scope, fixed price, and a repeatable delivery process. "AI invoice automation: I set up automated processing for your vendors in 2 weeks for $2,500." Because the scope and process are standardised, each delivery is faster and more profitable than a bespoke build, and it's *much* easier to sell (clients understand exactly what they get). Turning your best bespoke project into a productised service is often the single highest-leverage business move.

**Recurring revenue beats one-off fees.** One-off project fees mean constantly hunting for the next client. **Recurring revenue**, monthly maintenance/monitoring retainers, hosting and support, "automation-as-a-service" subscriptions, builds a stable base. Your Week 17 observability skills make this natural and honest: clients happily pay a monthly fee for you to *run, monitor, and maintain* their automations (keep them working, handle changes, fix breakages). Building recurring revenue into your offerings is what turns sporadic project income into a sustainable business.

Today: take your strongest/most-repeatable automation and design it as a **productised service**, a fixed scope, a fixed price, a standardised delivery process, and a **recurring** maintenance/monitoring component. Write the one-paragraph offer as you'd present it to clients. Even if you sell custom work first, having this productised offering ready is what lets your business scale beyond your hours.

items.title: Day 6 - Selling automation services
items.body:
## Consolidate: your end-to-end client engagement

Today you connect the week into a coherent picture of *how an automation business actually runs*, from finding a client to delivering and maintaining, so you have a repeatable engagement model, not just disconnected sales tips.

**Map the full client journey.** Lay out your end-to-end process: **find** (outreach/platform/referral) → **qualify & discover** (understand the real problem, frequency, cost, data, edge cases) → **scope & propose** (written deliverables, exclusions, timeline, value-based price, AI-reliability expectations) → **build** (using everything from the technical weeks) → **deliver** (deploy, document, hand off, train) → **maintain** (monitoring, support, retainer, the recurring revenue). Seeing the whole journey, and knowing you can execute each stage, is what makes "I can run an automation business" real rather than aspirational.

**Lean on the skills you've built for each stage.** Notice how the whole course supports this: opportunity-spotting (W1) finds work; the build skills (W2–W15) deliver it; deployment (W16) and observability (W17) make delivery reliable and enable recurring maintenance revenue. The business isn't separate from the technical, it's *built on* it. Your reliability and observability skills, in particular, are a *competitive advantage in sales*: "I don't just build it, I run it, monitor it, and you'll never find it silently broken" is a powerful, honest differentiator most freelancers can't offer.

**Professionalism is a multiplier.** Across every stage, the soft skills compound: clear communication, honest expectation-setting, written scopes, reliable delivery, responsive support. These make clients *trust* you, which drives repeat business and referrals, the lifeblood of a sustainable practice. Many technically-weaker builders out-earn stronger ones purely on professionalism and trust. Treat client management as a core skill, not an afterthought.

**Define your offering and your next action.** Pull it together into a clear statement of what you offer and to whom: your niche, your productised service(s), your pricing approach, your recurring component. Then define the single next concrete action to get a real client, send proposals, message warm contacts, post your offering, because the business only becomes real when you *do* the outreach. Week 19 gives you a real project to deliver; this consolidation is the framework you'll run it within.

Today: write your **one-page business model**, your niche/offering, your end-to-end engagement process (find → discover → scope → build → deliver → maintain), your pricing approach, and your recurring-revenue component, plus the *one* concrete outreach action you'll take this week to land a real client. You now have both the skills *and* the model to turn them into income.

items.title: Day 7 - Selling automation services
items.body:
## Ship it: your automation business toolkit

Wrap Week 18 with a committed **business toolkit**, the sales-and-delivery assets that turn your technical skills into income.

**What to ship.**
- An **outcome-led portfolio** (3–5 case studies, problem → solution → result → how, with at least one tangible demo).
- A **focused offering**: your niche, a productised service (fixed scope/price/process), and a recurring maintenance/monitoring component.
- A **sales kit**: a specialised profile/pitch, a discovery-questions list, and a scope/proposal template.
- A **one-page business model** (engagement process, pricing approach) and a concrete outreach plan.

**How to ship it.**

```bash
git add business/ README.md
```

(Keep client-sensitive material private; commit the templates and your own assets.)

This toolkit, a proof-of-work portfolio, a clear offering, a repeatable sales-and-scoping process, and a business model that includes recurring revenue, is what converts your capability into a livelihood. The builders who succeed aren't always the most technical; they're the ones who can find a real problem, scope it honestly, deliver reliably, and maintain trust. You now have the framework to be that person.

Next week you put it *all* together on something real: a **client project**, delivering a working automation that processes real data for a real person (a paying client, a free-for-case-study build, or a real business you know). Theory becomes a delivered result.

items.title: Choose your project
items.body:
## Choose your project: a real automation for a real person

This week is the point of the entire course: you deliver a **real automation that solves a real problem for a real person**. Not a tutorial, not a demo on toy data, a working system that someone *other than you* uses on *real* data. This is the difference between "I learned automation" and "I built automation that's actually being used", and it's the most valuable thing in your portfolio.

**The one hard requirement.** The automation must be **used by someone other than you** and must **process real data**. Within that, your "client" can be: a real paying client (ideal), a business owner who agreed to a free build in exchange for a case study and testimonial (excellent, and a great way to land the first one), a family member's or friend's small business, or a real organisation you're part of. The point is *realness*, real beneficiary, real data, real stakes, because real surfaces the messy edge cases and the communication challenges that no practice project can.

**Choose a problem you can actually finish.** Apply the scoping discipline ruthlessly (W18): pick something genuinely useful but *bounded enough to deliver well in a week*. A sharp, finished automation that reliably saves someone 5 hours a week beats an ambitious half-built one every time. Better to nail a focused problem, "automate this specific recurring report", than to attempt a sprawling system and ship something broken. Narrow and done is the goal.

**Run real discovery first.** Before building, do the discovery (W18): sit with your "client", understand the *actual* current process, the data (where it lives, what format, how messy), the edge cases and exceptions, and what a good outcome looks like *to them*. Real processes always have surprises the brief didn't mention, the weird exception, the inconsistent data, the unstated requirement. Surfacing these now, not mid-build, is what lets you scope realistically and deliver something that actually fits their reality.

**Scope it in writing, set expectations.** Write the scope (deliverables, what's excluded, the AI-reliability expectation, w18). Agree it with your client. This protects you both and makes the project deliverable. Even for a free/friend build, a written scope keeps it focused and professional, and gives you the experience of doing it properly.

Today: **choose your client and project**, secure a real beneficiary with a real problem and real data, run a discovery conversation to understand the actual process and data, and write a clear, bounded scope you can deliver this week. Getting a *real, well-scoped* project locked in today is what makes the rest of the week a genuine professional deliverable.

items.title: Build, day 1
items.body:
## Build, day 1: data, design, and the spine

With a scoped project and real data in hand, today you start building, and the priority is the *foundation*: understanding the real data, designing the pipeline, and getting the core spine working. Resist polishing; prove the central flow first, because real data has a way of breaking assumptions.

**Confront the real data first.** Real client data is messier than any sample, inconsistent formats, missing fields, surprising edge cases, the exception nobody mentioned. Spend real time *understanding* it before building: load it, inspect it, find the dirty rows, the format variations, the cases that break the simple approach. This isn't a detour, the real data *is* the problem, and discovering its messiness now (rather than when the client tests it) is what lets you build something that actually works. Many a client project fails because the builder designed for the data they imagined, not the data that exists.

**Design the pipeline against reality.** Map the automation's flow, trigger → fetch → process (AI judgment) → act/deliver, with the *real* data and the *real* edge cases in mind. Where does the messy data get cleaned? Where do exceptions get handled or escalated? What's the failure path? Designing explicitly against the real data's quirks (not an idealised happy path) is what separates a robust delivery from a fragile demo. Use everything, the right altitude (no-code vs code), the right tools, the reliability patterns.

**Build the spine end-to-end.** Get the *core* flow working on real data before adding any polish: input → the key AI step (with structured, validated output) → output, producing a correct result on a real example. A working spine proves the approach is sound and de-risks the project early. Once the spine works on real data, you *know* the project is deliverable; everything after is hardening and refinement. Spine-first is how professionals avoid the trap of polishing pieces of a system that doesn't yet hold together.

**Check in early if needed.** If the real data reveals the scope needs adjusting (a much bigger edge-case problem than expected, missing data you assumed existed), surface it with the client *now*, not at the deadline. Early, honest communication about a scope issue is professional and builds trust; a silent struggle ending in a missed deadline does the opposite. Real projects sometimes need re-scoping; handling that well is itself a skill.

Today: **build the foundation**, deeply understand the real data, design the pipeline against its actual messiness, and get the core spine working end-to-end on a real example (correct, validated output from real input). By end of day, the central flow should run; you'll harden and complete it over the next two days.

items.title: Build, day 2
items.body:
## Build, day 2: harden, handle edges, make it reliable

With the spine working, today you make it *reliable*, the unglamorous, essential work of handling the edge cases, failures, and messiness that real-world use will throw at it. This is where a demo becomes a deliverable, and it's exactly the engineering most amateurs skip (and then their automation breaks the first day a client uses it).

**Handle the real edge cases.** Yesterday's data exploration surfaced the exceptions, the malformed records, the missing fields, the unusual formats, the cases the happy path doesn't cover. Now handle each deliberately: validate inputs and outputs, deal with the messy/missing data sensibly, and decide what happens for cases the automation *can't* confidently handle (flag for human review, the human-in-the-loop pattern). An automation that handles the client's *actual* edge cases is one they can trust; one that only works on clean examples will embarrass you on day one.

**Layer in the full reliability stack.** Apply everything from the course: enforced **structured output** with validation (W5), **error handling** so one bad item doesn't crash the run (W8), **retries** for transient API/network failures (W13), **idempotency** so re-runs are safe (W2/W10), and sensible **fail-loud** behaviour for the unrecoverable. Each guard removes a class of failure. For a system someone *relies on*, this reliability isn't optional polish, it's the core of the value you're delivering.

**Build in the human-in-the-loop where it matters.** For anything consequential or uncertain, design the human checkpoint honestly: the automation handles the confident majority and *escalates* the rest for quick human review, rather than silently guessing. This is what makes AI automation *safe* for real business use, and setting the client's expectation accordingly ("it'll auto-handle ~95% and flag the rest for you") is the honest, trust-building approach. A well-designed escalation path is a feature, not an admission of weakness.

**Test against reality, hard.** Run the automation against a *realistic* set of the client's actual data, including the nasty cases, and fix what breaks. Better still, test the edge cases *you know* exist in their data. The goal: by end of day, the automation reliably produces correct results on the real, messy data it'll face in production, not just on the clean example from yesterday. This honest stress-testing is what lets you deliver with confidence rather than crossed fingers.

Today: **harden the automation**, handle the real edge cases, layer in the full reliability stack (validation, error isolation, retries, idempotency, fail-loud), build the human-in-the-loop escalation for uncertain cases, and stress-test against real, messy data until it reliably produces correct results. A robust, edge-case-handling automation is the actual deliverable; this is the day that earns the trust.

items.title: Build, day 3
items.body:
## Build, day 3: complete, refine, and prepare to deliver

Today you complete the automation, refine the output to genuinely fit the client's needs, and get it ready to hand over. The build is nearly done; this day is about the finishing that makes it not just *work* but actually *delight* the person who'll use it, because their experience of it determines whether you get the testimonial, the referral, and the repeat work.

**Complete the full scope.** Finish every piece of what you scoped: the trigger, the processing, the *delivery* (the output landing where and how the client needs it, a report in their inbox, rows in their spreadsheet, records in their system). The automation should now do the *whole* job end-to-end, not just the interesting AI part. Clients judge the complete experience, an automation that processes perfectly but dumps output somewhere inconvenient hasn't actually solved their problem. Close the loop fully.

**Refine the output to fit *their* world.** The output is what the client actually experiences, so make it fit how they work: the right format, the right place, clear and usable, matching their existing process rather than forcing them to adapt to yours. If they live in a spreadsheet, deliver to their spreadsheet in their layout. If they want an email summary, make it clear and skimmable. This client-centric refinement, shaping the output to *their* reality, is often what turns "it works" into "this is exactly what I needed", the difference between a satisfied client and a delighted one.

**Make it usable and maintainable by them.** Consider the human on the other end: is the human-review queue (for escalated cases) easy for them to use? Is it obvious when something needs their attention? Can they understand what the automation did? An automation that requires *you* to operate it isn't truly delivered; one the client can use confidently on their own is. Smooth the rough edges that would confuse a non-technical user.

**Final end-to-end verification on real data.** Before you call it done, run the *complete* automation on real data one final time and verify every stage: correct trigger, correct processing, correct handling of edge cases, and correct delivery to the right place in the right format. This full dress rehearsal catches the integration issues that piece-by-piece testing misses. The automation should now reliably do the entire job, on real data, ready for the client's hands. (Deployment and documentation come tomorrow, W16/W17 skills applied.)

Today: **complete and refine the automation**, finish the full scope including delivery, refine the output to fit the client's actual workflow, make it usable by them, and do a final end-to-end verification on real data. By end of day you should have a *complete, polished, working* automation that does the whole job, ready to deploy and hand over.

items.title: Deploy and document
items.body:
## Deploy, document, and hand over

A working automation on your laptop isn't a *delivered* automation. Today you deploy it so it runs reliably for the client, document it so it can be trusted and maintained, and hand it over professionally, the steps that turn "I built it" into "the client has a working solution they rely on". This is the culmination, and how you deliver shapes the relationship as much as what you deliver.

**Deploy it to run for real.** Apply your W16 deployment skills: get the automation running where it needs to (cloud server, scheduled job, webhook service), with secrets managed properly, the correct trigger configured, and *verified working in production* (not just "deployed"). The client needs it to run reliably without you babysitting it, that's the whole point. A "finished" automation that only runs when you manually start it on your machine hasn't been delivered. Make it genuinely operational in the client's world.

**Add observability so it's trustworthy and maintainable.** Apply your W17 skills: structured logging, error alerting (so *you* find out if it breaks), and a health check/heartbeat. This isn't just good practice, it's what lets you honestly promise "I'll know if it breaks before you do", and it's the foundation for a recurring maintenance relationship. An observed automation is one you can confidently stand behind; an unobserved one is a liability waiting to surprise you both.

**Document for handover.** Write documentation the *client* can use: what the automation does, how to use it (especially the human-review parts), what to do if something looks wrong, and how to reach you. And keep technical documentation (how it's deployed, its config, how to maintain it) for yourself or whoever maintains it. Good handover documentation is what makes the automation a durable asset rather than a black box only you understand, and it signals professionalism that drives repeat business.

**Hand over professionally, and set up the relationship.** Walk the client through it: show it working, explain how they interact with it, demonstrate the review process, answer their questions, and make sure *they* feel confident using it. A good handover (a short call or screen-recording walkthrough) makes the client feel supported, not abandoned. This is also the natural moment to discuss ongoing **maintenance/monitoring** (the recurring revenue from W18), "I'll keep it running, monitored, and updated for a monthly fee", turning a one-off project into an ongoing, sustainable relationship.

Today: **deploy, document, and hand over**, get the automation running reliably in production (verified), add observability (logging, alerting, health check), write client-facing and technical documentation, and do a professional handover that leaves the client confident using it. Then propose the ongoing maintenance relationship. You've now *delivered* a real automation, the complete arc from problem to running solution.

items.title: Day 6 - Client project, build a real automation
items.body:
## Consolidate: reflect on delivering real work

The build is delivered; today you extract the *lessons* from doing it for real, because the gap between practising automation and *delivering* it to a real person teaches things no tutorial can, and capturing those lessons is what makes your *next* project better.

**Reflect honestly on the experience.** Real delivery is different from practice in instructive ways. What surprised you? Where was the real data messier than expected? Where did the scope strain, or an unstated requirement appear? How did the human factors, communication, expectation-setting, the client's actual workflow, shape the work? Writing down these honest observations turns a single project into durable, transferable lessons. The surprises are the curriculum; the discomfort is where you grew.

**Assess against the outcome that matters.** The real measure isn't "did the code work" but "did it solve the client's problem and save them what you promised?" Evaluate honestly: Is it actually being used? Is it reliably saving the time/effort you projected? Is the client genuinely better off? This outcome focus, value delivered, not features built, is the mindset that makes you valuable, and the metric you'll lead with in your case study and future sales. If it fell short, understanding *why* is more valuable than pretending it didn't.

**Capture the case study and testimonial now.** While it's fresh, document this as a portfolio case study: the problem, your approach, the *result* (quantified, "saved ~8 hours/week", "processes 200 documents/day at 98% accuracy"), and ideally a **testimonial** from the client. This is gold, a *real* delivered project with a real result and a real client's words is the single most persuasive thing in your portfolio, worth far more than any course-built demo. Ask the client for the testimonial while their satisfaction is fresh; it's the asset that wins your *next* clients.

**Identify what to improve and what to reuse.** What would you do differently next time, in discovery, scoping, building, or handover? And what's *reusable*, could this become a productised service (W18), is there a pattern here you'll see again? Both directions matter: the improvements make you better, and the reuse makes you faster and more scalable. This reflection is how one project compounds into a growing, improving practice rather than an isolated job.

Today: **write your project retrospective**, honest lessons from delivering real work (the surprises, the real-data mess, the human factors), an outcome-based assessment of the value delivered, a polished **case study with a client testimonial**, and notes on what to improve and what's reusable/productisable. You've not only built real automation, you've learned from delivering it, which is what turns a first project into a career.

items.title: Day 7 - Client project, build a real automation
items.body:
## Ship it: a delivered, real-world automation

Wrap Week 19, the course's true capstone, with a **real automation, delivered to a real person, processing real data, in production**.

**What you've shipped.**
- A **working automation** solving a real problem for a real beneficiary, on real data, that they actually use.
- Built properly: scoped from genuine discovery, hardened against the real edge cases, with validation, error handling, and human-in-the-loop where it matters.
- **Deployed and running** in production (verified), with **observability** (logging, alerting, health check) so it's trustworthy and maintainable.
- **Documented** for both the client and maintenance, with a professional handover done.
- A **case study with a quantified result and a client testimonial**, and ideally an ongoing maintenance arrangement.

**How to ship it.**

```bash
git add client-project/ README.md
git commit -m "Week 19: delivered client automation (real user, real data, deployed, documented)"
git push
```

(Commit your documentation, code, and case study; keep client-confidential data and credentials private.)

**Why this matters.** This is the proof that you can do the job, not learn about it, *do* it. A real, delivered, in-use automation with a quantified result and a client testimonial is worth more than every practice project combined. It's the centrepiece of your portfolio, the strongest possible answer to "can you actually deliver?", and, if it's a paying or productisable project, the first step of a real business. You've gone the full distance: from "what is AI automation?" in Week 1 to a delivered, running, real-world system.

Next week, the finale: **portfolio and what's next**, making your work visible, positioning yourself in the market, and planning your path forward in a field that's only accelerating.

The AI automation space moves fast, what is advanced today becomes a commodity in 12 months. ## Zero-cost path (no credit card required)

This week mentions industry-standard tools that can cost money. You can complete every step for free, with no card and no trial that auto-renews:

- **LLM calls**, use **Ollama** (runs Llama 3 / Mistral locally, free, no API key): point the base URL at `http://localhost:11434`. The chat shape is identical; you just swap the endpoint. Hugging Face's free Inference API also needs no credit card.

items.title: Polish your GitHub
items.body:
## Polish your GitHub: your public proof of work

You've built a lot, real automations, a deployed client project, production-grade systems. Now you make it *visible and credible*, starting with GitHub, where technical clients and employers look to verify you can actually do the work. A polished GitHub turns "trust me" into "see for yourself", and most people leave it a mess, so polishing it is easy, high-leverage differentiation.

**The profile README: your front page.** GitHub lets you pin a **profile README** (a special repo named after your username) that shows on your profile homepage. Make it a sharp introduction: who you are ("I build reliable AI automations for businesses"), what you do, links to your best projects and your portfolio/contact. This is the first thing a visitor sees, treat it as a landing page, not an afterthought. A strong profile README instantly signals you're serious.

**Curate and pin your best repos.** Quality over quantity, ruthlessly. **Pin** your 4–6 strongest projects (the client project, the RAG system, the research agent, the document processor) and make sure the rest don't drag down the impression. A visitor should see a curated set of impressive, well-documented work, not a graveyard of half-finished experiments. Archive or tidy the noise; lead with your best.

**Every pinned repo needs a great README.** For a BI/automation portfolio, the **README is the project**, most visitors read it and never open the code. Each pinned repo's README should have: what it does (the problem and outcome), a **screenshot or demo GIF/video** (tangible proof), how it's built (the approach and tech), and how to run it. A repo with a clean, outcome-led README and an embedded demo is worth ten repos with bare code. Invest here, it's what gets read.

**Signal professionalism throughout.** The details that mark a serious builder: meaningful commit histories (which you've built all course), clean repo structure, no committed secrets (verify!), clear documentation, and consistent quality. These signals, more than any single project, tell a technical evaluator "this person works professionally". The polish is the message.

Today: **polish your GitHub**, write a strong profile README (who you are, what you build, links), pin your 4–6 best projects, ensure each pinned repo has an outcome-led README with a demo/screenshot, verify no secrets are committed, and tidy the overall impression. A clean, curated GitHub is a powerful, always-on proof of competence, make it represent your best.

days.title: Write 3 case studies
days.summary: A case study turns a project into a sales document.

items.title: Write 3 case studies
items.body:
## Write 3 case studies: turn projects into persuasion

Raw projects show *what* you built; **case studies** explain *why it mattered and what it achieved*, which is what actually persuades clients and employers. A good case study turns a technical artefact into a compelling story of value delivered. Today you write three, your most persuasive sales and credibility assets.

**The case-study structure.** Each follows a clear arc: **The Problem** (the business pain, quantified, "the team spent ~15 hours/week manually processing invoices, error-prone and slow") → **The Approach** (what you built and key decisions, accessibly explained) → **The Result** (the outcome, *quantified* wherever possible, "cut it to ~1 hour/week of review, 98% accuracy, ~$1,500/month saved") → **The How** (the technical detail, for those who want it). Lead with problem and result, the value, then support with approach and tech. This problem-result-first structure is what makes a case study persuasive rather than just descriptive.

**Quantify the value, this is the whole point.** The most persuasive element is a *concrete number*: hours saved, error rate reduced, cost cut, volume handled, turnaround improved. "Saved ~15 hours/week" or "processes 500 documents/day at 98% accuracy" is far more convincing than "improved efficiency". Automation is *especially* good for this because its benefits are so measurable, lean into it. Even for non-client projects, frame the realistic value the solution *would* deliver. Numbers turn interest into belief.

**Pick three that show range.** Choose three projects that together demonstrate **breadth**: ideally your real **client project** (the strongest, with a testimonial), plus two others showing different capabilities, a document-processing or RAG system, an agent, a deployed pipeline. Together they should say "I can solve a *range* of automation problems, reliably, end to end". Range reassures a prospect that you can handle *their* particular problem, whatever it is.

**Make them tangible and accessible.** Include screenshots, demo videos, before/after, and write in plain, outcome-focused language a non-technical decision-maker can follow (they're often the buyer). A case study peppered with jargon loses the very person who'd hire you. Show the result, tell the story simply, and let the tangible proof (the demo, the number, the testimonial) do the convincing.

Today: **write three polished case studies** (problem → approach → result → how), each led with a quantified outcome, written accessibly, with tangible proof (screenshots/demo), and chosen to show range, ideally anchored by your real client project. Add them to your portfolio site. These three documents are your most persuasive assets for landing the *next* client or job.

items.title: Reflect on the 20 weeks
items.body:
## Reflect on 20 weeks: from zero to delivering real automations

Before planning ahead, look back, deliberately, at how far you've come. Reflection isn't sentimental; it's how you consolidate scattered skills into a clear, confident sense of *what you can now do*, which is exactly what you need to articulate to clients, employers, and yourself. Twenty weeks is a real transformation; own it.

**Take stock of the arc.** You started with "what is AI automation?" and you can now: orchestrate workflows in n8n; write Python automations; call AI APIs reliably with structured outputs; engineer prompts for production reliability; build autonomous agents; scrape the web and process documents with AI; automate email and data; build with LangChain and LangGraph; implement RAG over private knowledge; automate browsers; deploy to production; monitor and operate systems; *and* sell, scope, and deliver to real clients. That's a genuinely deep, end-to-end capability, builder, deployer, operator, *and* businessperson. Few people have all of it.

**Recognise the durable skills beneath the tools.** Specific tools (n8n, LangChain, whichever platform) will change, what's permanent is the *judgment* you've built: spotting automatable opportunities, choosing the right altitude (no-code vs code vs agent), designing for reliability, knowing AI's limits and where humans belong, and delivering value to real people. These transferable skills are your real asset; they'll outlast every tool in this course and let you adapt as the field shifts. Name them, they're what you're really selling.

**Acknowledge the proof you've built.** You don't just *know* this, you have *evidence*: a portfolio of real automations, a deployed client project with a quantified result and testimonial, production systems you built and operate. This proof is what separates you from the vast number of people who've "played with AI". You've *shipped*, repeatedly, to real standards. Let that calibrate your confidence honestly: you're not a beginner hoping to break in; you're a builder with a body of delivered work.

**Be honest about gaps, too.** Reflection includes seeing what's still weak, the areas you found hard, the skills you'd want to deepen, the kinds of projects you haven't tackled yet. This honest self-assessment isn't discouraging; it's the input to a smart learning plan (tomorrow) and the mark of a professional who knows their own envelope. Knowing what you *don't* yet know well is as valuable as knowing what you do.

Today: **write a reflective stock-take**, the full arc of what you can now do, the durable judgment-skills beneath the tools, the concrete proof you've built, and an honest assessment of your remaining gaps. This clear-eyed picture of your capability is the foundation for confidently positioning yourself, and for the forward plan you'll build next.

items.title: Your 30-day plan
items.body:
## Your 30-day plan: turning capability into momentum

Skills fade and momentum dies without a concrete next-step plan. The riskiest moment after finishing a program is the drift that follows, so today you build a specific, actionable **30-day plan** to convert everything you've learned into real-world traction, clients, income, or a job, while the momentum and the skills are fresh.

**Choose your immediate direction.** First decide what the next 30 days are *for*: landing freelance clients, getting hired into an automation/AI role, building a productised service, or deepening specific skills toward a bigger goal. You can't pursue everything at once, and a focused 30 days beats a scattered one. Pick the primary direction that best fits your situation and goals, and orient the plan around it. (You can adjust later; the point is to *move*.)

**Make it concrete and action-based, not vague.** A real plan is specific actions with deadlines, not aspirations. For freelancing: "Week 1: finalise portfolio and profile; send 10 proposals. Week 2: 10 more + 5 warm-contact messages. Week 3: discovery calls, scope a project. Week 4: deliver, get a testimonial." For job-hunting: applications sent, people contacted, projects polished, interviews prepared, all with numbers and dates. Concrete, measurable actions are what actually get done; "improve my portfolio" doesn't. Build the plan as a checklist you execute.

**Front-load the highest-leverage actions.** Some actions matter far more than others, *outreach* (proposals, applications, messaging warm contacts) and *visible proof* (portfolio, case studies) drive results; endless tweaking and tutorial-watching feel productive but don't. Put the high-leverage, slightly-uncomfortable actions (especially outreach, which most people avoid) *first* and in quantity. The plan should be weighted toward the actions that actually produce clients or interviews, not the comfortable ones. Doing *enough* outreach is usually the deciding variable.

**Build in accountability and review.** A plan without accountability slips. Set a way to track it (a simple checklist, weekly review) and ideally make it *visible* (tell someone, post your goal, find an accountability partner). Plan a weekly check: what did I do, what worked, what's next? This keeps the 30 days on track and lets you adjust based on real feedback (which proposals got responses? which message landed?). Momentum compounds when you maintain and review it.

Today: **write your concrete 30-day plan**, your chosen direction, specific weekly actions with numbers and deadlines (front-loaded with outreach and visible-proof tasks), and an accountability/review mechanism. Then *start* on today's first action. The plan only works if you execute it, so begin now, while the skills and momentum are at their peak.

items.title: What to learn next
items.body:
## What to learn next: staying ahead in a fast field

AI automation moves *fast*, what's advanced today is a commodity in a year. The good news: your competitive edge was never knowing one specific tool; it's your ability to *identify opportunities, design reliable systems, and deliver them*. Those transfer. Today you set a smart learning direction so you keep growing and stay ahead, without chasing every shiny new thing.

**Anchor on the durable, adapt the specifics.** The field's churn is real, models, frameworks, and platforms change constantly, but the *fundamentals* you built are stable: opportunity-spotting, reliability engineering, knowing AI's limits, system design, and delivery. Keep these sharp and you can absorb any new tool quickly. So your learning strategy is: stay *fluent* in fundamentals, and learn new specifics *as projects require them*, not by chasing hype. This keeps you current without the exhausting treadmill of learning every new release.

**Promising directions to deepen.** Depending on your goals, high-value next areas include: **deeper agentic systems** (multi-agent collaboration, more sophisticated planning and tool use); **evaluation and reliability** (rigorously measuring and improving AI system quality, an increasingly critical, underserved skill); **specialised domains** (going deep in a vertical, legal, finance, healthcare automation, where domain expertise + automation is highly valuable); **MLOps/LLMOps** (operating AI systems at scale); and **the business side** (sales, productisation, building a team or product). Pick directions that fit *your* goals, not a generic "learn everything" list.

**Specialise to stand out.** As AI automation becomes mainstream, *generalists* become common and *specialists* command premiums. Consider developing depth in a niche, a specific industry's automation needs, a particular hard problem (complex document understanding, reliable autonomous agents), or a productised offering. Specialisation makes you the obvious choice for that problem and is harder to commoditise than general "I do automations". You don't have to specialise immediately, but be alert to where you could go deep.

**Build durable learning habits.** Staying current is a *habit*, not an event: follow a *few* high-signal sources (not the entire firehose), *build* with new capabilities when a project warrants (hands-on beats reading), keep reflecting on your own work, and learn from each project. The builders who thrive long-term aren't those who learned the most in one course; they're those who *keep* learning efficiently and applying it. A sustainable, signal-over-noise learning habit is what keeps your edge sharp for years.

Today: **set your learning direction**, identify the durable fundamentals to keep sharp, choose 1–2 next areas to deepen (aligned to your goals), consider where you might specialise, and define a sustainable learning habit (your few key sources, your "learn-by-building" rule). A deliberate learning strategy is how you stay valuable in a field that won't stop moving, by riding the change rather than chasing it.

items.title: Day 6 - Portfolio and what's next
items.body:
## Consolidate: position yourself and commit to action

On this final consolidation day, you bring everything together into a clear *position* in the market and a firm commitment to act, because all the skill and all the portfolio in the world produce nothing without positioning and execution. This is where you turn "I finished the course" into "I'm launching".

**Define your positioning crisply.** Pull your reflection, portfolio, and learning direction into a sharp answer to "who are you and what do you offer?" The strongest positioning is *specific*: "I build and operate reliable AI automations for [type of business / problem], document processing, data workflows, reporting, so they save hours and run themselves." A crisp, specific position makes you memorable, referable, and the obvious choice for your niche, far better than a vague "I do AI stuff". Write your positioning statement and use it everywhere, profiles, pitches, your portfolio homepage.

**Ensure your proof matches your position.** Your positioning is only credible if your visible work backs it up. Check the alignment: does your portfolio, GitHub, and case-study set clearly demonstrate the thing you say you do? If you position as a document-automation specialist, your strongest, most visible pieces should be document automations. Tighten any gap between what you *claim* and what you *show*, the proof must match the pitch, or the pitch falls flat.

**Commit to the execution, with accountability.** You have the skills, the portfolio, and the plan; what remains is *doing it*, and this is where most people falter, retreating to more tutorials instead of the uncomfortable work of outreach and shipping. Commit firmly to your 30-day plan, with real accountability (a partner, a public commitment, a tracked checklist). The single biggest predictor of whether this course changes your life isn't your skill level, it's whether you *execute* the outreach and keep shipping. Decide now that you will.

**Internalise the core truth, you are a builder who delivers.** The mindset to carry forward: you're not someone hoping to break into AI automation; you've *built* real systems, *deployed* them, *operated* them, and *delivered* to a real client. You have proof. Approach the market from that position of demonstrated capability, not as a hopeful beginner. That earned confidence, grounded in real shipped work, is what lets you charge fairly, pitch boldly, and persist through the inevitable early rejections. You can do this; you've already proven it.

Today: **finalise your positioning** (a crisp, specific statement of who you are and what you offer), **verify your proof matches it**, and **make a firm, accountable commitment** to execute your 30-day plan. Then take the very first action today. The course gave you the capability; this commitment is what turns it into a career.

cards.prompt: The fastest way to learn a new tool is to read the docs end-to-end before writing any code.
cards.whenRight: Right - building a tiny example first beats reading every page.
cards.whenWrong: Docs are a reference, not a tutorial. Code first, read second.

cards.prompt: Committing small checkpoints helps you debug regressions and review your own progress.
cards.whenRight: Exactly - tiny commits are a superpower.
cards.whenWrong: They really do help; `git revert` is one command away.

cards.prompt: Copy-pasting from Stack Overflow without understanding is a sustainable long-term strategy.
cards.whenRight: Correct - understanding the why is what makes you employable.
cards.whenWrong: Short-term it works; long-term it stalls you.

items.title: Day 7 - Portfolio and what's next
items.body:
## Ship it: your launch-ready portfolio and plan

This is the final ship of the program, package everything into a **launch-ready professional presence** and commit to the path forward.

**What to ship.**
- A **polished GitHub** (strong profile README, 4–6 pinned projects each with an outcome-led README and demo, no secrets, professional throughout).
- **Three case studies** (problem → approach → quantified result → how), anchored by your real client project, on a clean **portfolio site**.
- A **crisp positioning statement** (who you are, what you offer, your niche) used consistently across your profiles.
- A **concrete, accountable 30-day plan** and a **learning direction** for staying ahead.

**How to ship it.**

```bash
git add portfolio/ case-studies/ plan/ README.md
git commit -m "Week 20: launch-ready portfolio, case studies, positioning, and 30-day plan"
git push
```

**Why this matters, and what you've become.** Over 20 weeks you went from "what is AI automation?" to building, deploying, operating, and *delivering* real automations to real people, with the business skills to turn that into income. You have rare, valuable, end-to-end capability *and* the proof to back it. Most people who "learn AI" never ship a single real thing; you've shipped many, including a delivered client project with a quantified result.

The capability is built; the proof is visible; the plan is set. What remains is execution, the outreach, the proposals, the next build, the persistence. Approach it as what you now demonstrably are: a builder who delivers reliable AI automation. The field is accelerating and the demand is enormous; you're equipped to meet it.

Go build automations that run businesses without human hands, and get paid for it. You're ready.

items.body:
[PRODUCE] Tag your work as v20.0 and push to GitHub. The commands below stamp a versioned release of this week's work:

```bash
git add . && git commit -m 'Portfolio and what's next'
git tag v20.0 && git push --tags
```
